title: Social work informatics: an equity framework for health informatics.
source: PubMed · Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
desc: [Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA] Social work informatics (SWI) was proposed as a professional specialty in 2006, yet social work remains under-represented in health informatics governance, research, and system design even as artificial intelligence (AI) shapes high-stakes clinical decisions. This paper introduces the SWI Equity Framework, positioning social work as a leader in designing equitable health informatics systems. The framework was developed through a synthesis of social work, health informatics, and health equity literature. The framework identifies 6 domains: reflexive system co-design, social determinants of health data integration, training-data quality and representation, contextual interpretation of AI outputs, community leadership, and equitable accountability. The framework highlights opportunities to integrate social work expertise throughout the health informatics lifecycle, moving beyond consultation toward active participation in system design, implementation, and governance. It also outlines pathways for advancing social work informatics through education, interdisciplinary research, health systems, and professional infrastructure. Social work is particularly well positioned to advance the equity agenda of health informatics and offers profession-specific expertise that can strengthen equity, accountability, and implementation across the informatics lifecycle.

title: Multimodal AI for bacterial vs viral upper respiratory tract infection multicentre development and internal validation
desc: Distinguishing Group A streptococcus (GAS) pharyngitis from viral upper respiratory tract infections (URTIs) is critical for appropriate antibiotic use but remains difficult on symptoms alone. We developed and internally validated a multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) model fusing pharyngeal images (Swin Transformer) with clinical metadata via gradient boosting decision trees, using 6666 visits and 119,988 images from 44 facilities collected March 2023–August 2025. For discriminating GAS from non-GAS (influenza A/B, COVID-19), the fusion model achieved area under the curve (AUC) 0.917 (95% confidence interval 0.907–0.926), outperforming image-only (0.902), metadata-only (0.871) and proxy Centor/McIsaac scores. At a pre-specified high-specificity threshold (≥0.90) sensitivity was 0.761; simulations indicated antibiotic-prescription reductions of 23–56% across GAS prevalences of 5–20%. External validation and prospective evaluation are needed.

title: Artificial intelligence and machine learning: Shaping the future of venous thromboembolism diagnosis and prognosis.
desc: [Artificial intelligence in medicine] Venous thromboembolism (VTE) continues to pose a substantial health issue worldwide, characterized by high rates of mortality and morbidity. The field of artificial intelligence (AI) has shown potential as a valuable asset for enhancing the detection and prediction of complex diseases, such as VTE. This review explores the role of AI in VTE prediction and diagnosis, analyzing various machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) approaches, including natural language processing (NLP), support vector machines (SVM), random forests (RF), logistic regression (LR), gradient boosting methods, and deep learning frameworks such as ClotCatcher. Among the artificial intelligence models, those based on natural language processing algorithms, particularly ClotCatcher, demonstrated strong performance in analyzing unstructured clinical data. ClotCatcher achieved exceptional Area under the Curve (AUC) values of 0.980 and 0.995 for venous thromboembolism (VTE) adjudication from radiology reports. AI-driven methodologies facilitate early detection, personalized risk assessment, and enhanced patient outcomes. AI holds great potential for improving VTE diagnosis and risk assessment, offering greater accuracy and efficiency than traditional methods. However, further studies are required to validate these models across diverse populations and clinical environments. The integration of AI in VTE management represents a promising frontier in personalized medicine, potentially leading to improved outcomes and more efficient healthcare delivery.

title: Reliability Information and Physicians' Treatment Decisions in Sepsis With Respiratory Failure
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Nanjing University; conditions: Sepsis; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 40; status: ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING] * This study will examine whether showing predicted consequences alongside an artificial intelligence (AI) treatment recommendation affects physicians' decisions about intravenous fluids and vasopressors for patients with sepsis. The AI system compares the current treatment plan with alternatives and predicts how the patient's condition may change under each plan. It may recommend a change when the predicted benefit is consistent across several plausible assumptions; otherwise, it states that the evidence is insufficient to recommend a change. * About 72 physicians from two hospitals will review 30 retrospective, de-identified intensive care decision points. In the first stage, each physician will make treatment decisions without AI information. In the second stage, physicians will review cases under three conditions: the case with the on-duty clinician's plan but no AI information (B0); the same information plus an AI recommendation (B1); and the same recommendation plus predicted consequences for the current and recommended plans (B2). The conditions will be assigned across case blocks using counterbalanced sequences. Physicians will be stratified by clinical seniority, without specifying years of experience. * Final decisions will be compared with treatment plans independently made by an expert panel. The study will estimate differences in decision quality across conditions; the direction and size of any differences are unknown. No patients will be enrolled or treated, and physicians' study decisions will not affect patient care.

title: Separating Measurement Failures from Defence Failures in Split Language-Model Privacy
desc: Split-training privacy evaluations fail through distinct mechanisms. Evaluators can overlook an exposed gradient channel, align reconstructions against shifted labels, or deploy uncalibrated probes before testing a candidate defence, while calibrated attacks can also refute real defences. Separating these failure modes alters which claims survive. We conduct a retrospective evidentiary reanalysis across four split-LLM campaigns and two cross-cutting scope checks covering host key custody and variational mutual-information bounds, mapping every recorded claim to one of five admissibility states (breach, non-detection, undetermined coverage, invalid measurement, or out-of-scope inference). Across a 19-configuration exploration, only four of 24 required probes qualified, yet those four calibrated probes still established qualified privacy breaches in 13 configurations, while utility or learning-gain failures eliminated the remaining 6. In a seven-cell defence-redesign pilot, 2 quantised configurations failed utility gates, calibrated next-byte structure probes breached the 0.02 gate on all 7 cells (0.097 to 0.112), and qualified punctuation-property probes reached 0.79 to 0.89, yielding 4 failed and 3 undetermined composite privacy assessments (the latter from marginal null-band excursions on punctuation bindings). Negative evidence against both defence families remains intact. Scope checks further show that shared-key orthogonal wrappers protect passive network captures without hiding activations from a compromised restoring host, and why near-zero variational lower bounds leave worst-case leakage unconstrained. Rerunnable scripts verify 1,522 checks across 122 SHA-256-pinned artifacts while preserving each campaign's native seed intervals and retrospective boundaries.

title: InterGenEHR$^+$: An Interactive Framework for Natural Language-Conditioned Generation of Longitudinal Patient Trajectories
desc: Objective: To develop and validate InterGenEHR$^+$, an interactive framework for natural language-conditioned generation of synthetic tabular electronic health records (EHRs) and longitudinal trajectories for scenario-based evaluation of machine learning models. Methods: An optional large language model (LLM) parser converts clinical requests into structured constraints. Conditional variational autoencoders and diffusion models generate single-time-point records, while diffusion models generate longitudinal trajectories. We evaluate parsing, distributional fidelity, imputation, clinical-constraint adherence, mortality prediction, and clinical plausibility using a multi-institutional cohort of 874 patients receiving venovenous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV-ECMO). Results: Gemma 3 4B with few-shot prompting achieves the highest parsing performance with a low spurious slot rate. IGE-TabDDPM and IGE-PMVAE perform well in single-time-point generation; IGE-CSDI, IGE-FGTI, and IGE-MTSCI lead on different longitudinal fidelity metrics. Across five random seeds and three classifiers, synthetic cohorts retain predictive utility for mortality prediction on real test data. Clinician ratings support trajectory plausibility and alignment with requested scenarios. Conclusion: InterGenEHR$^+$ supports clinician-specified generation of EHR trajectories with statistical fidelity and downstream predictive utility in the evaluated VV-ECMO cohort. Extension to other clinical settings requires further validation. Significance: The framework supports scenario-based evaluation of machine learning models in data-sparse critical care settings.

title: Deep Learning Prediction of DNA Damage Response Protein Signaling from H&E Histopathology and Reverse-Phase Protein Arrays in Pan-Gynecologic and Breast Cancers

Routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) slides are available for nearly every patient. This project asked whether H&E morphology carries information about functional DDR protein signaling across five cancer types in a single model. We matched 1,673 diagnostic whole-slide images from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) to Level 4 reverse-phase protein array (RPPA) data for 1,527 patients with breast (BRCA, n = 858), endometrial (UCEC, n = 403), cervical (CESC, n = 146), ovarian (OV, n = 72), and uterine carcinosarcoma (UCS, n = 48) tumors. Slides were tiled at 0.5 m/px and Macenko-normalized, yielding 20.4 million tiles. Tiles were embedded with two frozen pathology foundation models, UNI2-h and Virchow2. A gated attention-based multiple instance learning (ABMIL) network jointly regressed six RPPA pathway scores, including a DNA_damage composite of 11 DDR proteins. Performance was assessed by out-of-fold Spearman correlation under 5-fold, cancer-type-stratified, site-grouped cross-validation and compared against a baseline that predicts each patient's cancer-type mean. title: An Explainable Analytics Framework for Identifying Process Deviations in Emergency Care for Patients with Multiple Long-Term Conditions
desc: Patients with Multiple Long-Term Conditions (MLTCs), also known as multimorbidity, often present clinical and operational challenges in emergency departments (EDs), yet how their care pathways deviate from expected workflows remains underexplored. This study introduces a process-aware analytical framework that quantifies and interprets ED process deviations by integrating multi-perspective conformance checking with explainable machine learning. Using routinely collected Scottish ED data between 2017-2023, we derived an empirical benchmark pathway. We introduced a new metric, the deviation score (DS), which captures both structural misalignments and breaches of the four-hour ED standard, a national service target defined as completion of ED care within four hours of arrival. Compared with non-MLTC attendances, MLTC patients exhibited longer and more complex pathways, higher DS values, and lower conformance to the benchmark model. The framework enabled interpretable SHAP analyses, revealing that deviation severity among MLTC attendances was primarily associated with triage acuity, year of attendance, activity queue length (number of patients queuing for the same care activity), and referral source, with additional contributions from age, arrival time, and number of chronic conditions. Threshold effects were observed in both queue length and multimorbidity burden, beyond which deviation severity increased sharply, suggesting points where standard pathways become harder to maintain. These findings show that deviation severity for MLTC patients is shaped by clinical urgency and system-level pressures at presentation. However, the inherent complexity of MLTC patients may further increase vulnerability to deviation. The framework offers the potential foundation for process evaluation and targeted improvement in emergency care.

title: Later-born generations have better memory and lose it more slowly
desc: Dementia risk at any age has been falling for decades. An analysis of ~219,000 people followed for up to 30 years shows that newer generations start old age with a larger cognitive capacity that declines more slowly than that of previous generations, and this combined advantage is large enough to account for the fall in dementia incidence.

title: Potential of multimedia-supported informed consent in clinical practice: a systematic review
desc: Providing targeted, quality-assured patient information is essential for informed and autonomous decision-making but remains resource-intensive when delivered face-to-face. Multimedia-supported informed consent may enhance patient understanding and satisfaction while reducing physician time by complementing, rather than replacing, direct interaction. Our PRISMA-based systematic review, aiming to enable clinicians to implement and evaluate such a supplement, identified 907 articles of which 110 reports from OECD countries were included, including 62 randomized controlled trials. Among studies assessing the outcomes of interest, 71% reported improved patient understanding with multimedia tools compared to standard consent, 41% reported increased patient satisfaction (none reported decreases), and 91% found reduced or unchanged patient anxiety. In synthesis, to the extent possible despite substantial heterogeneity, findings suggest benefits and potential efficiency gains, and we were able to derive recommendations. However, considerable methodological variability and limitations affecting internal validity highlight the need for high-quality head-to-head comparative studies to draw more robust conclusions.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Large Language Models Across the Heart Failure Care Pathway: A Narrative Review.
desc: [Journal of personalized medicine] Heart failure affects more than 64 million people worldwide and remains associated with high mortality and recurrent hospitalisation. Artificial intelligence (AI), including large language models (LLMs), is being evaluated across the care pathway, but evidence maturity varies by task. The aim of this narrative review was to appraise direct evidence for LLM applications in heart failure, distinguish it from supporting evidence for other AI methods and propose a risk-based framework for clinical evaluation and governance. The strongest direct LLM evidence concerns electronic health record extraction, document drafting, patient information and clinical trial endpoint adjudication. A small, randomised pilot evaluated supervised generative-AI-guided optimisation of guideline-directed medical therapy. Prospective case-finding and monitoring evidence largely concerns non-LLM AI. For conversational AI telemonitoring (a natural language interface with rule-based alerting), prospective evidence was limited to a single non-randomised controlled pilot. Performance depends on task definition, data completeness, human review and workflow adoption. Overall, LLMs can support clearly defined, supervised heart failure tasks, but current evidence does not justify autonomous high-stakes care. The evidence base is expanding but predominantly retrospective. Prospective trials, disease-specific benchmarks, equity assessment and regulatory engagement are prerequisites for safe clinical translation. Human oversight remains essential across all current-generation applications.

title: AI Agent Based on Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Nurses' Management of Postpartum Hemorrhage
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Beni-Suef University; conditions: Postpartum Hemorrhage, Clinical Competence; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 62; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] The goal of this randomized controlled trial is to find out whether an artificial intelligence (AI) agent based on retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves nurses' performance in managing postpartum hemorrhage (PPH). The participants are registered nurses working in the obstetric and gynecological ward, the obstetric emergency department and the critical care unit of Kafr Elsheikh General Hospital, Egypt. The main questions it aims to answer are: 1. Do nurses who use the RAG-based AI agent achieve higher performance scores in simulated PPH scenarios than nurses who use a printed guideline? 2. Do nurses who use the agent achieve higher PPH knowledge scores, complete more critical actions and perform them faster? Researchers will compare the intervention group, which receives PPH education plus training on and four weeks of access to the AI agent, with the control group, which receives the same PPH education and a printed guideline booklet based on the World Health Organization (WHO) 2025 recommendations. Participants will: * Complete a PPH knowledge questionnaire and perform a video-recorded simulated PPH scenario at baseline, immediately after the training and after four weeks. * Attend educational sessions on PPH (both groups) and training sessions on the AI agent (intervention group only). * Use the AI agent in daily practice for four weeks (intervention group only) and rate its usability at the end of the study.

title: Small Learned Projections for Semantic-Reversal-Aware Retrieval with Spectral Acceleration: A Four-Domain Empirical Study
desc: Dense-embedding retrievers can fail adversarially: when a query is answered by a document A and reversed by a near-copy B that differs from A by a small meaning-changing edit (a "trap"), raw cosine over E5-Large-v2 places B in the top-10 for 82-100% of queries at a pool of 5,000. We study two things. First, a small learned projection W: R^1024 -> R^d (d in {11, 32}), trained by a deterministic recipe on a declared set of cases, that suppresses the trap: for the declared cases, HN@10 = 0.0000 (no trap in the top-10) in all twelve (domain, pool-size) settings across four independent domains (legal, medical, patent, financial) and pools up to 100,000, while the correct paraphrase is retained for 93-99% of cases, under exact nearest-neighbour search. Second, a boundary-conditioned accelerator that serves the projection at that scale: an acceleration of spectral graph retrieval (SpectRAG) that replaces a dense eigendecomposition with a boundary-value solve, holding HN@10 = 0.0000 at n = 100,000 in every domain and retrieving the ~300-query suite in 0.6-1.1 s (~2-4 ms per query on average). Because the lens's output is the stored representation (a few floats per document), a hardened, specialised index per domain or tenant is ~90x smaller and dimension-proportionally faster than the full embedding, making many small declared indexes a practical alternative to one large vector store. The claim is scoped to the declared cases on the measured pools, with no probabilistic bound; the correct-answer rate drops for a reworded query against an unchanged corpus (about 0.79, trap suppression still holding). A projection transfers only partly to other domains, which we report in full. The recipe, lenses, trap sets and evaluation harness are released under AGPL-3.0; the accelerator's implementation is a reserved commercial component, and every HN number is reproducible under exact search.

title: JHealthBench-L: Clinician-Reviewed Localization of HealthBench for Rubric-Based Medical LLM Evaluation in Japan
desc: Rubric-based benchmarks such as HealthBench evaluate large language models (LLMs) on open-ended health consultations using case-specific physician criteria, many of which presuppose the healthcare institutions, medications, and care pathways of their source region. Under machine translation alone, these regional assumptions remain in the rubric, leaving responses appropriate in Japan uncredited or falsely penalized under foreign clinical rules. To adapt established clinical evaluation perspectives to Japan without authoring rubrics from scratch, we construct JHealthBench-L (79 patient-facing consultations, 1,022 criteria) through source-cited LLM drafting, single-specialist selection and revision, independent dual-physician review, and meta-review. Specialists rewrote only 4.4% of criteria from scratch, and independent reviewers approved 93.6% of Stage-2 criteria without issue. Comparing JHealthBench-L with a machine-translated baseline across 18 LLMs reveals that translation-only evaluation preserves coarse model rankings ($τ= 0.817$, mean shift +0.027) yet flips verdicts on 17.7% of modified criteria (vs. 7.3% re-grading noise) and reduces false penalties on Japan-adapted negative criteria by 7.1 percentage points, masking item-level clinical mismeasurement behind stable leaderboards. Axis-level and paired analyses further show that context awareness and Japan-specific clinical criteria remain primary bottlenecks, whereas Japanese continual pretraining and reasoning post-training substantially improve locally grounded performance. Datasets, physician revision logs, and evaluation code are available at https://github.com/horshohei/JHealthBench-L.

title: An interpretable framework for decoding transcriptomic foundation models
desc: Background: What transcriptomic foundation models encode, and how well they describe cells and tissue on targeted spatial panels, is under-explored. It is unclear whether a concept-labeled sparse autoencoder (SAE) feature represents its concept or only the genes it detects. Results: Here, we propose interpreTFM, which decomposes frozen transcriptomic foundation model activations with SAEs. We applied it to a CosMx lung-cancer section, four further CosMx donors, and a Xenium renal-cell-carcinoma section. On held-out tokens of known genes, sparse features marked 262--593 concepts per analysis layer, and SAEs of re-initialized scGPT and Geneformer did as well. On held-out genes, concept F1 was 0.01--0.12 for every representation and lowest for sparse features. A linear probe of hidden states predicted the concepts of unseen genes, but only in trained models. Per cell, sparse features reached 66--98% of single-gene population specificity (57--110% in the donors). In the analyzed CosMx section, sparse-feature niches matched author cell types at ARI 0.34--0.42, while expression-only niches reached 0.30; in the donors, their defining concepts recurred but their composition did not. In Xenium, the niches shared by all models were recovered from expression alone. Calibrated model interface calls were at chance in CosMx and tracked transcript spillover in Xenium. Conclusions: On these panels, SAE features act as concept-labeled gene detectors, while learned concept information is distributed across hidden dimensions. Concept labels should be checked against held-out genes and re-initialized models. For cells and niches, the features give named descriptions, comparable across models and patients and bounded by the measured panel.

title: Making Invisible Infrastructure Visible: Data Landscapes Across a National Pain and Opioid Research Network through a Qualitative Assessment
desc: Background Multi-site research networks have become central infrastructure for NIH-supported health research, yet network-level coordination has focused on harmonization, common data models and FAIR principles, while rarely characterizing the heterogeneous data landscapes within a network first. The Helping to End Addiction Long-term(R) Initiative (HEAL Initiative) Data2Action (HD2A) program comprises ten autonomously designed innovation and acceleration projects in opioid use disorder treatment and pain management, with no pre-existing network-level view of what data each project used or how it was governed. Objectives To make the HD2A data-infrastructure landscape visible by systematically characterizing the data environments of all ten projects and identifying cross-project themes, coordination opportunities, and lessons for multi-site networks. Methods Data Infrastructure Support Center staff extracted each project's data-environment characteristics from project documentation into a structured 15-element assessment, which project investigators reviewed and corrected. Two analysts independently coded the ten validated assessments (two-pass inductive content analysis; 19-code codebook), developed six cross-project themes from the coded passages by consensus, and judged each project against them. An investigator reflection survey, summarized descriptively, contextualized the document-based findings. Results Six themes characterized the landscape: all projects integrate multi-source, cross-sector data; dashboards are the common data-to-action venue; adoption of standards-based interoperability is uneven; governance complexity increases nonlinearly with institutional partners; implementation and improvement science frameworks serve as data-quality scaffolding; and sustainability plans depend on institutional transfer. Five synergy clusters were identified. Investigators consistently described data access and governance, not analytic capability, as the binding constraint, and distinguished sustaining technical products from sustaining their use. Conclusions Making a networks data infrastructure visible is not a substitute for harmonization but a prerequisite for deciding how and what to harmonize. HD2As autonomously designed projects share a common structure of constraints, creating opportunities for coordination without uniformity. The structured elicitation approach is replicable in other innovation networks.

title: A systematic review and meta analysis of extended reality interventions for chronic respiratory conditions
desc: Extended reality (XR) is increasingly used in rehabilitation but its effectiveness in chronic respiratory conditions remains unclear. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of experimental studies comparing XR-based interventions with usual care or alternatives. Searches were performed from inception to March 2025 and risk of bias was assessed by two independent reviewers. Fifteen experimental studies were included. XR-based interventions significantly improved 6-min walk distance (mean difference [MD] = 29.90 meters), forced vital capacity (MD = 0.37 liters), reduced dyspnea (standardized mean difference [SMD] = −0.61), anxiety (SMD = −2.08), and depression (SMD = −1.10), and improved quality of life (SMD = −1.87). No significant effects were observed for forced expiratory volume in one second percent predicted or fatigue. Subgroup analyses showed stronger effects in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and with comprehensive XR programs. Exercise-based XR improved quality of life only, while activities of daily living simulations improved forced expiratory volume in one second percent predicted, and nature-based interventions showed no significant benefit. Heterogeneity was substantial, but sensitivity analyses confirmed robustness of primary outcomes. XR-based rehabilitation may improve exercise capacity, symptoms, and quality of life, but larger multicenter trials are required to confirm long-term effectiveness and cost-effectiveness.

title: Performance of a mammography-based deep learning risk model across breast cancer tumor phenotypes.
desc: [European radiology] Breast cancers have diverse biologic features associated with variable prognoses, treatment selection, and eligibility for targeted therapies. We evaluated the discriminatory performance of an image-only deep learning (DL) breast cancer risk model across diverse tumor phenotypes, including histologic subtypes, grades, molecular profiles, and disease stages. This retrospective, multisite study included consecutive women 30 years or older undergoing screening mammography across six sites from 2009 to 2022. A previously validated image-only DL model (Mirai) was used to generate risk scores from screening mammograms. Demographic data were retrieved from electronic health records, and cancers diagnosed within 1 year were identified through linkage to regional and state tumor registries. Discrimination across histologic subtypes, grades, molecular profiles, and stage was evaluated using areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUCs), with DeLong comparisons. Among 341,921 examinations in 104,472 patients (median age, 59 years [IQR, 51-68]), 1991 cancers were diagnosed, including 1543 (77.5%) invasive cancers and 448 (22.5%) ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS). Discrimination was similar for invasive cancer (AUC 0.81; 95% CI: 0.80-0.82) and DCIS (AUC 0.81; 95% CI: 0.79-0.83; p = 0.88) and did not differ between invasive ductal and lobular carcinomas (AUC 0.81 vs 0.78; p = 0.08). Discrimination was robust across grades for both invasive cancer and DCIS (AUC range, 0.79-0.83), molecular profiles (AUC range, 0.77-0.88), and stages (AUC range, 0.71-0.82). Screening mammograms contain imaging biomarkers associated with diverse breast cancer phenotypes. An image-only DL risk model demonstrated robust discrimination across histologic subtypes, grades, molecular profiles, and disease stages. Question Does an image-only mammography-based deep learning breast cancer risk model (Mirai) demonstrate similar performance across breast cancers with different phenotypes? Findings In a multisite cohort of 341,921 screening mammograms, Mirai demonstrated similar discrimination across invasive cancer and ductal carcinoma in situ and maintained robust performance across histologic subtypes, tumor grades, molecular profiles, and stages at diagnosis (AUC range, 0.71-0.88). title: ReFocus: Progress-Guided Adaptive Practice for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation Reinforcement Learning
desc: Online reinforcement learning (RL) enables vision-language-action policies to improve through environmental interaction. However, in long-horizon manipulation, sparse success/failure feedback provides little information about where policies encounter bottlenecks. Moreover, repeated full-task rollouts also leave these bottlenecks weakly analyzed and insufficiently practiced. To this end, we introduce ReFocus, a progress-guided multi-round RL framework that alternates between Global and Local RL to identify task-specific bottlenecks and allocate additional practice to them. Specifically, during Global RL, we decompose each task into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of subtasks. Then a DAG-based Progress Reward is leveraged for both policy training and bottleneck diagnosis. Based on the identified bottlenecks, ReFocus selects Adaptive Practice Windows, defining task segments from an entry stage to a target stage. It allocates additional interaction to these segments during Local RL while updating the entire policy. After that, it evaluates the policy to perform the full task for the next round of RL, forming an iteration between Global and Local RL. Experiments on LIBERO-Long and RoboCasa365 show that ReFocus achieves success rates of 97.8% and 51.3%, respectively, compared with 90.6% and 39.3% for the π_{0.5} baseline. Furthermore, we evaluate a real-world adaptation on three long-horizon tasks. On BreadBaker, ReFocus achieves 95% success, compared with 30% for the π_{0.5}. Project page: https://refocus-robotics.github.io.

title: TAT-Det: A Dataset for Testicular Appendage Torsion Detection and Segmentation in Ultrasound Images
desc: Background: Testicular appendage torsion (TAT) is the leading cause of acute scrotal pain in prepubertal children. Yet, its diagnosis remains challenging due to nonspecific clinical manifestations and the absence of standardized datasets for pediatric acute scrotal emergencies. Results: We present TAT-Det, an expert-annotated ultrasound dataset specifically designed for TAT. TAT-Det comprises 2,600 ultrasound images from 1,203 patients collected at the Children's Hospital, Zhejiang University School of Medicine. Each TAT-positive image is accompanied by lesion-level bounding boxes for detection and pixel-level segmentation masks for fine-grained delineation. Annotations were produced through a multi-stage workflow involving independent annotation by board-certified pediatric sonographers, consensus review, and refinement. Baseline benchmarks for object detection and semantic segmentation using representative deep learning models are further provided, with YOLO11m achieving the best detection performance and RWKV-UNet the best segmentation performance. Conclusions: TAT-Det addresses the lack of publicly available resources for pediatric emergency ultrasound and establishes a foundation for developing and evaluating artificial intelligence methods for automated TAT analysis.

title: XenoType: Decoding cellular identity in breast cancer histology through molecular supervision
desc: Characterizing the cellular composition of the tumor microenvironment from histological images is fundamental to understanding cancer biology and informing treatment decisions. Deep learning has enabled automated nuclear detection and classification from hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) images, yet cell classifiers remain largely confined to broad morphological categories owing to a reliance on manual annotations. Recent efforts have used spatial molecular measurements to supervise histological classification, but these approaches often require separate tissue sections or produce altered H&E staining, and the resulting cell-type annotations depend on subjective choices such as marker selection and clustering parameters. Here we develop XenoType, a framework that classifies cells into seven molecularly informed categories directly from routine histology, trained using paired same-section Xenium spatial transcriptomics. Cell-type annotations are reconciled from four single-cell RNA-sequencing references, reducing dependence on marker choices. Across eight held-out breast tissue sections, XenoType outperformed commonly used CellViT++ retrained on the same molecular annotations under both four-class (macro-F1: 0.703 vs. 0.569) and seven-class (macro-F1: 0.571 vs. 0.403) taxonomies, with the largest gains for myoepithelial (F1: 0.175 to 0.572) and endothelial cells (F1: 0.395 to 0.682). Molecular measurements are required only during training; at inference, XenoType uses the H&E image alone. Model-reference agreement increased consistently with annotation confidence, and XenoType generalized to an independently profiled breast tissue section from a different spatial transcriptomics platform, supporting scalable cell-type mapping from routine histology without per-specimen molecular profiling.

Sequential framework for predicting postoperative recurrence and antiseizure-medication withdrawal risk in mesial temporal lobe epilepsy
desc: Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (mTLE) is a common drug-resistant epilepsy. Temporal lobe resection is the most effective treatment, but postoperative recurrence and antiseizure medication (ASM) withdrawal remain major clinical challenges. Existing prediction tools are limited by endpoint specificity, restricted external validation, and lack of integration into sequential postoperative management pathways. We developed a sequential modelling strategy in mTLE, spanning recurrence prediction to ASM withdrawal risk stratification. In phase 1, postoperative recurrence models were developed and validated using 52 preoperative multimodal features in 1278 patients across cohorts 1–4 (three retrospective, one prospective). Five top-ranked models achieved AUCs of 0.926–0.932 (internal) and 0.830–0.931 (three external sets), with a three-tier (low/intermediate/high) risk stratification. In phase 2, ASM withdrawal recurrence models were developed and validated in 679 seizure-free, phase 1 low/intermediate-risk patients eligible for withdrawal across cohorts 5–8 (three retrospective, one prospective). Five top-ranked models achieved AUCs of 0.897–0.902 (internal) and 0.789–0.933 (three external sets), with risk stratification for individualized withdrawal estimation. Models showed good calibration, net clinical benefit, and SHAP-based interpretability. A research-based risk-estimation web tool was developed to support potential clinical translation. This promising modelling strategy integrates population-level risk stratification with individualized prediction, providing preliminary postoperative guidance: high-recurrence-risk patients may not be ideal for early ASM withdrawal despite seizure freedom, while low-risk patients may be considered for earlier withdrawal evaluation. Given the primarily retrospective design and relatively small phase 2 prospective cohort, further prospective external validation and clinical-impact studies are required before routine implementation.

title: Artificial Intelligence in the Multidisciplinary Tumor Board for Prostate Cancer: A Narrative Review.
desc: [Current oncology (Toronto, Ont.)] Multidisciplinary tumor boards (MDTs) guide prostate cancer decisions but are strained by rising case volumes, evolving guidelines, and growing complexity. Artificial intelligence (AI) now enters the MDT at two levels. First, it generates inputs: deep-learning magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reading matches or exceeds radiologists' performance in the Prostate Imaging-Cancer Artificial Intelligence (PI-CAI) study; Gleason grading reaches expert-level agreement; PSMA PET quantification is automated; and multimodal pathology biomarkers predict ADT benefit. Second, decision-support systems act on MDT output: rule-based tools reproduce standard recommendations in 86-99% of cases, mostly in populations dominated by standard cases, whereas general-purpose large language models (LLMs) agree with real urological boards in 56-93% of cases, depending largely on input quality and case mix, and perform worse in metastatic disease; agreement does not establish clinical benefit. Of 33 appraised decision-support studies, 27 were at high risk of bias, 20 of them solely because the treating board served as an unblinded reference standard; explainability, regulation, and automation bias remain unresolved. We propose that AI currently serves as a supervised pre-reader, guideline checker, and triage tool. Prospective multicenter studies with patient outcomes are needed.

title: Project LEO (Learn-Execute-Overcome): An LLM-driven CBT Journalling Supporter to Reduce Procrastination Among Young Adults
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: The Hong Kong Polytechnic University; conditions: Procrastination; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 60; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] The goal of this three-arm randomised controlled trial is to learn if a large-language-model-driven CBT journalling supporter (LEO) can reduce procrastination among young adults (18 to 24 years) with General Procrastination Scale scores over 59. The specific aims of the research include: 1. Assess the feasibility and acceptability of LEO for addressing procrastination among young adults in Hong Kong, including adherence, engagement, and user satisfaction. 2. Evaluate LEO's effectiveness in supporting CBT-informed journalling, focusing on usability, frequency and completeness of entries, and the quality of reflective content. 3. Evaluate the preliminary effectiveness of LEO in reducing procrastination and improving mental well-being and functional outcomes, relative to control and active control conditions.

title: Did the Model Forecast It, or Already Know It? Evaluating Large Language Models for Novel Drug-Target Prioritisation with a Temporal Knowledge-Graph Oracle
desc: AI systems increasingly help decide which drug targets enter costly clinical trials. We recast each target-disease hypothesis as a dated event, the pair's first clinical trial. This lets us test whether a language model can forecast such events after its training cutoff, rather than recall events before it. We rebuild a dated biomedical knowledge graph as it stood at the end of each year from 2020 up to its newest version. We then ask six open language models, with and without this graph, which targets will enter a first trial for a disease the next year. Without retrieval, the models rank about as well as trial history, a count of each target's past trials in the same therapeutic area, also after their training cutoffs. Evidence dated before the decision adds at most a small gain, before or after the models' training cutoffs. The newest graph raises five of six models clearly above that baseline, but its paths usually include the answer: the pair's own trial, dated after the decision. Evaluations of target prioritisation should date both features and labels, with evidence from before the decision and outcomes after it.

title: A noise-corrected metric for evaluating spatial transcriptomics predicted from histology
desc: Deep learning methods that predict spatial transcriptomics from histology offer scalable molecular profiling of clinical cohorts. However, conventional correlation metrics overstate prediction quality across whole sections by crediting models for recognizing broad tissue regions, and understate fine-scale prediction quality because sampling noise dominates sparse RNA counts. To resolve this, we introduce the reproducible-signal correlation (RSC) metric. RSC randomly splits RNA counts into two halves to separate reproducible signal from sampling noise across spatial scales and within tissue regions or cell classes. Across 12 spot-level and three single-cell methods, RSC revealed that most models capture broad tissue patterns but largely miss differences between neighboring spots or cells, which whole-section correlation overlooks. Within malignant cells, RSC distinguished methods that genuinely capture part of the cell-to-cell heterogeneity from those whose scores across all cells were inflated by cell-type composition. Guided by RSC, we designed a pairwise difference loss between neighboring spots that improved fine-scale predictions on average across 11 models. RSC thus provides a foundation for benchmarking predictions, guiding model design and determining which spatial analyses histology can support.

Treatment Selection in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: A Conceptual Framework for Precision Therapy.
desc: [Journal of personalized medicine] Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains a major therapeutic challenge, with limited improvement in outcomes and substantial heterogeneity in treatment response. Systemic chemotherapy remains a cornerstone of treatment across disease stages, yet treatment selection, particularly in metastatic PDAC (mPDAC), is still driven predominantly by clinical characteristics, performance status, prior therapy, and a limited number of molecular biomarkers. The emergence of biomarker-directed therapies, including strategies targeting oncogenic KRAS alterations, demonstrates the potential of molecularly informed treatment selection but also highlights the need to identify which therapy is most likely to benefit an individual patient at a specific clinical decision point. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), multi-omics profiling, digital pathology, and prospective therapeutic trials provide an opportunity to develop comprehensive precision-treatment strategies. Existing AI approaches, including PASS-01/MULTIPL, PDACai, and CHAI, provide important foundations but remain constrained by limitations in prognostic versus predictive modeling, reliance on predominantly static or correlational representations, limited mechanistic interpretability, and incomplete integration of treatment effects and evolving tumor biology. In this narrative review, we propose a conceptual framework for individualized treatment selection in mPDAC that integrates multiscale biological and clinical data, mechanistic graph-based pathway representations, multimodal transformer models, and causal estimation of individualized treatment effects. This framework shifts AI-enabled precision oncology from static biomarker prediction toward mechanistically informed, uncertainty-aware, causally grounded treatment selection, with the potential to adapt as tumor biology, therapeutic options, and clinical evidence evolve. Although initially focused on mPDAC, the framework provides a generalizable architecture for individualized treatment selection across other biologically heterogeneous cancers.

title: Adaptive Versus Fixed Mobile Exercise in Preservice Teachers
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Turan International University; conditions: Physical Fitness; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 440; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] This four-center randomized trial compares two mobile exercise prescription policies in preservice teachers in Uzbekistan. Both groups use the same OptiForma application and exercise library for 16 weeks, with three nonconsecutive sessions per week. In the adaptive arm, prescribed active time is modified using rules based on completion, perceived exertion, symptoms and current fatigue. In the fixed arm, the initial prescription is retained, with the same safety reductions when required. The primary outcome is the number of fully completed 20-m shuttle-run segments at week 16. Physical fitness tests, practicum fatigue, adherence and harms are assessed separately. Follow-up continues through week 28.

title: DosePET: An Open-Source Dataset with 2100 Radiation Dose Maps for PET/CT
desc: Large collections of three-dimensional radiation dose maps linked to patient anatomy are needed to develop artificial intelligence (AI) models for personalized internal dosimetry in nuclear medicine, but access to such data remains limited. Here we present DosePET, an open-source dataset of 2,100 patient-specific absorbed-dose maps generated by Monte Carlo simulation of publicly available PET/CT examinations: 1,503 [18F]FDG examinations from ENHANCE.PET and 369 [18F]PSMA-1007 and 228 [68Ga]Ga-PSMA-11 examinations from PSMA-PET-CT-Lesions, acquired at five institutions with seven scanner models. For each examination, the CT was resampled to the native PET grid to build a voxelized patient phantom, the quantitative PET image defined the radionuclide source, and radiation transport was simulated with GATE version 9.4. Organ and tissue masks were generated from the CT with TotalSegmentator. Each study folder contains a NIfTI dose map integrated from scan time to infinity, 117 binary organ/tissue masks, a report of regional dosimetric quantities, including mean absorbed doses, dose conversion factors and scan-time dose rates, and simulation metadata. The total processing time was 1,542.4 hours. Python tools support selective downloading and conversion to scan-time dose-rate or dose-per-decay maps, and an agent skill guides pairing with the source PET/CT images. DosePET is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/eltzanis/DosePET.

title: SYNDRI: Context-aware removal of transcript spillover in imaging-based spatial transcriptomics
desc: Imaging-based spatial transcriptomics (ST) measures gene expression at single-cell resolution, but imperfect segmentation often misassigns transcripts between neighboring cells, a problem known as transcript spillover. This spillover is niche-dependent and can therefore confound downstream analyses that rely on niche-specific differential expression. True spillover cannot be directly quantified in experimental ST data, so existing correction methods infer contamination indirectly from transcript positions or expression structure. Here we introduce SYNDRI, a post-segmentation correction method that frames spillover detection as a supervised, gene-level classification task. We develop SYNDRI-SIM to generate labeled training data by simulating spillover between spatially mapped scRNA-seq profiles. SYNDRI uses a transformer to predict gene-level spillover probabilities conditioned on each cell's expression, identity, and local neighborhood, without requiring transcript-level coordinates or deconvolution. On held-out simulated data, SYNDRI achieves an AUPRC of 0.86, compared with 0.64 for the next-best method. Across MERFISH, CosMx, and Xenium datasets, SYNDRI achieves the highest aggregate performance across metrics of cell-type separation, reference similarity, and preservation of within-cell-type heterogeneity. In a CosMx lung cancer dataset, SYNDRI removes nearly all potentially contaminating tumor and macrophage markers from differential expression between tumor-associated and stromal fibroblasts while retaining native fibroblast markers. These results demonstrate the utility of learning from simulated spillover to improve the interpretation of spatial gene expression.

Artificial intelligence as a tool in primary care practice: From burnout to breakthrough.
source: PubMed · Canadian family physician Medecin de famille canadien
desc: [Canadian family physician Medecin de famille canadien] To provide family physicians with a practical overview of artificial intelligence (AI) applications in primary care practice and their potential to address burnout, improve workflow, support clinical decision making, and enhance patient care. A comprehensive narrative review of AI tools in primary care was conducted using peer-reviewed literature from PubMed, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar, with subject headings artificial intelligence and primary care, along with related terms. Relevant real-world pilot projects and case studies were hand-searched to identify those not captured through database searches. Canadian family physicians are facing rising levels of burnout, driven by overwhelming administrative demands and increasing patient complexity. With 1 in 4 Ontarians estimated to be without a family doctor in 2026, primary care is under considerable strain. AI tools-particularly those powered by natural language processing (NLP) and large language models (LLMs)-offer timely, practical solutions across 4 domains: ambient AI scribes to reduce documentation time and enhance patient-physician interaction; intelligent document processing and clinical summarization to streamline inbox management and information retrieval; clinical evidence synthesis LLMs to summarize medical evidence at the point of care; and AI clinical decision support systems to improve diagnosis and disease management. Real-world implementation in primary care demonstrates these tools can improve workflow efficiency, reduce time spent on paperwork, enhance adherence to clinical guidelines, and improve patient satisfaction. However, inaccuracies in AI-generated content, model bias, lack of transparency, and data privacy risks all require careful oversight. AI and NLP applications have potential to be timely tools that reduce strain and restore capacity for relational, person-centred care. Thoughtful adoption-guided by evidence-informed deployment, user-centred design, and regulatory safeguards-will be essential to ensure safe, equitable integration into primary care practice.

title: RadOncGym: An Agent-Based Framework for Radiotherapy Dose-Mimicking Optimization
desc: AI dose-prediction models generate patient-specific 3D dose distributions from patient anatomy, providing an important intermediate representation for automated radiotherapy planning. However, an AI-predicted dose must undergo downstream optimization to produce a physically constrained treatment plan, a process that requires balancing competing planning objectives. We present RadOncGym, an agent-based framework that enables an LLM agent to iteratively tune 12 planning-objective weights for dose-mimicking optimization. To reduce iterative evaluation cost, RadOncGym incorporates a surrogate verifier that provides rapid feedback while allowing the agent to decide when to request a full planning solve within a fixed solve budget. We evaluate RadOncGym on 60 OpenKBP head-and-neck patients, each paired with 10 predictions from OpenKBP-Opt dose-prediction sets, yielding 600 patient-prediction contexts per experimental configuration. Under RadOncGym's 16-turn setting with a three-solve budget, a GPT-5.6 Sol agent reduces mean clinical-criterion violation by 0.6131 Gy and improves DVH and dose scores by 0.5986 and 0.2204 Gy relative to leaving all 12 weights fixed at 1, outperforming all evaluated non-agent weight-tuning methods under the same solve budget. It remains competitive with the 16-solve variants of these methods while requiring 75.0-77.6% less normalized runtime. RadOncGym demonstrates the potential of LLM agents as optimization planners in downstream radiotherapy plan optimization and provides a public testbed for their systematic evaluation. Code and configurations are available at https://github.com/miaot-usc/RadOncGym.

title: GASTON-VI efficiently quantifies spatial axes and molecular gradients from multi-sample, multi-modal spatial-omics data
desc: Many tissues exhibit an underlying spatial axis along which fundamental biological processes occur due to continuous spatial gradients of cell type and molecular state. Modern spatial-omics technologies measure molecular features (e.g. gene/protein expression) at 100,000s-1,000,000s of locations within a two-dimensional (2-D) tissue slice, with large-scale atlases profiling multiple tissue slices of the same organ type across different individuals and biological conditions (e.g. healthy versus diseased). However, existing computational methods for identifying spatial molecular gradients are limited to small spatial transcriptomics datasets (1000s of cells) of a single tissue slice, while methods for integrating multiple samples do not explicitly model spatial axes nor spatial molecular gradients along such axes. Here, we present GASTON-VI, a variational inference (VI)-based deep learning model which efficiently learns an underlying spatial axis and spatial molecular gradients along this axis from multi-sample, multi-condition spatial-omics data of any molecular modality (e.g. transcriptomics, proteomics). GASTON-VI jointly learns (1) a spatial coordinate (the "isodepth") for each individual tissue slice and (2) 1-D spatial modality functions that describe molecular gradients along the isodepth for tissues of the same biological condition, while utilizing a latent variable model to account for batch effects. Further, GASTON-VI implements a statistical test for identifying molecules with differential spatial gradients across biological conditions (e.g. healthy versus diseased). On spatial transcriptomics and proteomics data from the intestine, tonsil, and liver, we show that GASTON-VI recovers spatial axes and molecular gradients along these axes more accurately and efficiently than existing methods. In particular, applied to large-scale spatial transcriptomics and proteomics atlases, GASTON-VI reveals differential spatial gradients of gene expression along the portal vein-central vein axis in fibrotic livers, and differential spatial gradients of protein abundance along the muscularis-lumen axis across different regions of the intestine. Software availability: GASTON-VI is available at https://github.com/chitra-lab/GASTON-VI.

Differential scanning calorimetry and artificial intelligence for analytical profiling of disease-related plasma thermograms.
desc: [Talanta] Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) is a systems-level thermodynamic tool for probing disease-related changes in complex biological fluids, yet clinical translation is hindered by challenges in thermogram interpretation, reproducibility, and data integration. DSC captures heat capacity transitions from multistate protein unfolding, reflecting collective stability landscapes of the plasma proteome. Pathological conditions can induce reproducible thermogram distortions, suggesting their utility as ensemble biomarkers beyond conventional scalar descriptors. Recent advances in ultrasensitive and microfluidic DSC have improved stability and reduced sample needs, while artificial intelligence enables extraction of distributed calorimetric features beyond melting temperature and enthalpy. Machine learning strategies-including statistical, kernel-based, deep learning, and physics-informed frameworks-help identify informative thermodynamic patterns. This review integrates thermodynamic principles, data-driven analytics, and clinical studies to assess DSC's capabilities and limitations. We further propose practical standardization and minimum-reporting frameworks for DSC acquisition, preprocessing, AI model development, and validation to improve reproducibility and cross-study comparability. Persistent issues such as inter-laboratory variability, cohort heterogeneity, small datasets, and regulatory hurdles continue to restrict routine use. Overall, combining DSC with AI offers a promising analytical framework for extracting clinically meaningful thermodynamic insights and advancing disease characterization.

title: Privileged On-Policy Distillation for Calibrated Alzheimer's Diagnosis With Missing Modalities
desc: Alzheimer's disease is diagnosed from clinical, biospecimen and imaging evidence, but few patients undergo every test. Because these modalities are complementary, a missing one has many plausible values. Most existing methods leave it out or train on one estimate, so their classifier never sees its other values, and the estimate is never checked against the diagnosis. We address both gaps with on-policy distillation: the model fills in the missing modalities itself, and teachers with information available only in training grade these fills. Our method, Graded Rollout Imputation with Privileged teachers, draws several fills, one modality at a time. An imputation teacher that knows the diagnosis grades each step, bringing the outcome into the imputation as statistical practice recommends. A diagnosis teacher that sees all real modalities supplies a soft target. Trained on fills that vary, the model learns a confidence that reflects what the missing tests leave open, and it diagnoses from a single rollout. On the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative cohort, it outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. On two external cohorts, it remains competitive in discrimination and, even after every method is recalibrated, its calibration error is level with the lowest on both. Added to three of these baselines, the teachers improve each of them. Our method offers a single, well-calibrated model for whatever combination of tests a patient has received.

title: VenusPheno: Transfer-Guided Task Grouping for Multi-Task Bacterial Phenotype Prediction
desc: Understanding how genomic information gives rise to bacterial phenotypes is a fundamental problem in biology. Genome-level prediction requires models that integrate information from thousands of proteins, while related phenotypes may share genomic signals. However, not all phenotype tasks benefit from being learned together, and suitable task groups can be difficult to define from biological knowledge alone. We present VenusPheno, a framework that combines multiple-instance learning over pretrained ProtT5 protein embeddings with transfer-guided multi-task learning. An attention-based Set Transformer aggregates the proteins in each genome into a genome-level representation. We evaluate VenusPheno on 14 binary phenotype tasks from 12,178 bacterial genomes using genus-disjoint splits. Under single-task training, VenusPheno outperforms computational, conventional machine-learning, and deep-learning baselines in terms of mean balanced accuracy. We then use leave-one-task-out analysis to estimate directed transfer relationship between phenotypes, revealing both beneficial and detrimental interactions. Grouping tasks based on these transfer relationships further improves mean balanced accuracy over independent training and joint training of all tasks. Although inferred without biological priors, the resulting groups are consistent with biologically plausible relationships among phenotypes. VenusPheno therefore combines accurate phenotype prediction with a data-driven strategy for determining which tasks should be learned together. The PyTorch implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/YJinling/VenusPheno.

Clinical decision support for precision dentistry: Trends and emerging prospects.
source: PubMed · Journal of the American Dental Association (1939)
desc: [Journal of the American Dental Association (1939)] Precision oral health requires clinicians to consider patient-specific clinical, biological, behavioral, imaging, and preference sensitive data when making clinical decisions. In routine oral health care, however, these data are often fragmented across electronic dental records, imaging platforms, diagnostic tests, narrative notes, and patient-generated sources. Clinical decision support (CDS) systems provide a mechanism for organizing these data and translating them into timely, evidence-informed recommendations at the point of care. A narrative review was conducted of peer-reviewed literature relevant to precision dentistry, CDS, dental informatics, artificial intelligence, biomarkers and omics technologies, and patient-generated health data. Priority was given to dental studies, which were supplemented by broader medical CDS literature when dental-specific evidence was limited. CDS systems can function as digital infrastructure and generate clinical recommendations based on patient-specific data using evidence-based knowledge and predictive analytics. In dentistry, CDS applications range from rule-based reminders and electronic quality measures to artificial intelligence-assisted radiographic interpretation, risk prediction, biomarker screening, and emerging multimodal platforms. The clinical readiness of these technologies varies substantially, and their value depends on data quality, validation, work flow integration, usability, interoperability, privacy safeguards, and clinician oversight. CDS systems can assist clinicians by offering evidence-based, personalized recommendations that synthesize pertinent and available information. These systems are crucial for practicing precision dentistry. Although efforts to enhance the adoption, usability, effectiveness, and acceptance of CDS systems continue, clinicians should always regard CDS systems as tools and retain full responsibility for their decisions and involve patients in the decision-making process.

title: Evidence-Aligned Benchmarking and Learning for Medical Video Language Models
desc: A medical video language model should answer from the visual evidence its question asks about. We find three places where this breaks down and address each with an approach we call MedEvidU. First, benchmarks reward answers that ignore the video: on one dataset, the position of a clip within its recording predicts the surgical step in 37% of questions, and a constant answer beats every trained model on a standard safety-assessment metric. We build MedVidBench-v2, 34 tasks from 18 surgical and clinical video datasets, in which prompts and metrics are audited with answers given without video, and which tests unseen hospitals and windows cut blindly from whole recordings. Second, common video encoders merge consecutive frames into shared tokens, so a question about one frame is answered from a blend of two. Query-slot inputs give each queried frame its own tokens at almost no extra cost. Third, a fine-tuned model has memorized its training questions, which leaves little to learn from. Label-matched question resampling (LQR) adds unseen questions about the same recordings while keeping the answer distribution fixed, in a final supervised epoch and in reinforcement learning. Together, these raise the grounding IoU of a 4B model from 30.4 to 44.4, above a supervised 27B model, and instrument grounding at an unseen hospital from 33.9 to 72.5. On blindly cut windows, event-presence accuracy improves by 5.5 points and localization F1 by 8.1 points. Project page: https://gaozhongpai.github.io/MedEvidU/

title: SPECTRE: A versatile data framework for integrating spectral, environmental, and ecophysiological trait data
desc: With the increasing availability of large datasets and the growing importance of artificial intelligence (AI), robust and sustainable data management systems have become essential for plant and ecosystem research. In particular, the integration of heterogeneous spectral data with plant functional traits and environmental measurements from multiple sensors poses a major challenge, requiring significant time investment and long-term planning. Here, we present SPECTRE (Spectral, Trait, and Remote-sensing Ecophysiology data framework), a versatile data framework based on simple, open data formats that addresses the need of many research groups for a standardized organization of heterogeneous datasets, facilitating their integration and joint analysis without relying on proprietary software or external service providers. SPECTRE integrates a wide range of datasets linking spectral measurements to plant traits, including LiDAR, hyperspectral imagery, chlorophyll fluorescence, geospatial data, soil moisture, climate variables, and ecophysiological traits, organized into three main categories: (i) unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-acquired data, (ii) ground-based trait measurements, and (iii) environmental data. All datasets are stored using a standardized folder structure and converted to comma-separated values (CSV) format. A unified primary key enables consistent linking of spectral signatures to functional traits across datasets by species and site, facilitating trait-based analyses, data framework extension, and long-term usability. The widespread use of lookup tables reduces data redundancy and facilitates the integration of data with different naming conventions, while the use of Markdown for metadata and documentation ensures easy access to information without relying on complex or proprietary formats, simplifying documentation creation and maintenance. Overall, SPECTRE offers a simple, transparent, and scalable solution that can be readily adopted by plant ecophysiological laboratories, facilitating future AI-driven trait prediction analyses.

Explainable CNN Ensemble with AI-Generated Reporting for Fungal Infection Diagnosis.
desc: [Journal of fungi (Basel, Switzerland)] The need for precise classification of fungi from microscopic images plays a critical role in diagnosing and treating patients since it requires timeliness and effectiveness. Nevertheless, manual examination is time-consuming and difficult due to the similar visual features of numerous fungi. Therefore, this work proposes a new approach to explainable deep learning for fungal image classification and report generation. The developed framework consists of four pre-trained convolutional neural network models-DenseNet121, ResNet18, VGG16, and InceptionV3-which are used to classify fungal microscopic images into five classes. To make the process more transparent, methods such as Grad-CAM, SHAP, LIME, and Canny edge detection are used to identify the areas of images that contribute to the prediction. At the same time, the developed approach uses the large language model LLaMA3-70B through LangChain and provides automatic generation of the structured diagnostic report, including fungal identification, confidence scores, and clinical observations. The whole pipeline is implemented using the Streamlit interface to predict and generate a PDF report of the classification. The experiments have been performed using publicly available data containing 5000 images of fungi with expert annotations. Among the models analyzed, DenseNet121 shows the highest result, reaching an accuracy of 99.75% and having the values of precision, recall, and F1-score close to 0.998.

title: CHD-Bench: Diagnosing Congenital Heart Disease through Interactive Examination
desc: Diagnosis of congenital heart disease (CHD) requires understanding the spatial relationships between cardiac structures, which clinicians assess by scrolling through CT or cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) slices and rotating 3D reconstructions. Although automated methods have advanced cardiac segmentation, identifying congenital heart defects from volumetric scans remains an open challenge. The two existing approaches rely on handcrafted diagnostic rules limited to static anatomical abnormalities. We introduce CHD-Bench, the first benchmark for interactive CHD diagnosis, defining a multi-label task and evaluation protocol over 247 CT and MRI scans from three cohorts covering 38 CHD types. We also present CHD-Harness, open-source software that runs a VLM in a 3D Slicer environment through 22 tools, manages each examination, and records the resulting diagnosis and supporting views. We evaluate off-the-shelf medical, open weight, and closed weight VLMs and compare them with a 3D CNN classifier and published rule-based results. Gemini 4 Argon with CHD-Harness achieves the highest macro F1 across all three cohorts (0.63, 0.63, and 0.43). Allowing for interactive examination raises its macro F1 by up to 20 points over static views. These results establish CHD-Bench and CHD-Harness as a foundation for developing and evaluating VLMs for interactive CHD diagnosis.

title: Does embedding impact classification performance ? A small sample perspective
desc: Deep learning (DL) methods can address many challenges posed by high-dimensional and sparse microbiome data. In this study we applied and compared deep (DNN) and shallow (SNN) feedforward neural networks combined with five dimensionality-reduction techniques: Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF), Autoencoder based Embeddings (AE), and convolutional layers (Conv). To establish baseline classification performance, the XGBoost was used, as it represents a robust machine learning based classifier with a relatively low number of hyperparameters. The task was to classify effective microorganism (EM) treatments based on intestine bacterial family abundance in common carp. In particular, the experiment involved 25 ponds that were divided into experimental groups. In each pond, the intestinal microbiome of five individuals was determined by sequencing two hypervariable regions of the gene encoding the 16s rRNA gene sequencing. The sequence reads were processed by QIIME2 and taxonomically annotated to the SILVA database, what resulted in 126 annotated families that were used as features in all downstream analyses. Abundance tables from 125 samples, transformed using the Centered Log-Ratio (CLR) method, were used to evaluate ten dimensionality-reduction and Deep learning configurations considering five-, three-, and two-classification scenarios. The DL models were optimized using cross-validation. To combat the overfitting that was present due to sparsity and small sample size, dropout and kernel regularization were implemented. During testing autoencoder embeddings achieved the highest classification accuracy (0.84), exceeding the XGBoost baseline (0.64), while embedding based on convolutional layers significantly reduced performance (0.44). PCA and SVD transformations showed comparable results (0.65), whereas NMF often failed to converge, likely due to incompatibility with CLR-transformed data. Best classification results were obtained for models that implemented AE embedding, it is most likely caused by their ability to capture non-linear patterns in the data. All models showed stable training behavior, with loss functions consistently decreasing across epochs. The SNN models were markedly less computationally intensive, than DNN. AE and NMF based embeddings were the most resource hungry (Wall Clock Time and RAM). Our results show (1): SNN architectures performed slightly worse than DNN, du

title: Annotation-Free Vision-Language Concept Bottleneck Models for Interpretable Medical Image Classification: A Review.
desc: [Journal of imaging] Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) route predictions through a layer of human-understandable concepts, but classical CBMs need a concept label for every training image, a cost that is high in medicine. Vision-language models (VLMs) remove that requirement because, in a shared image-text embedding space, a large language model can propose candidate concepts and contrastive similarity can score them, with no concept labels. This review surveys annotation-free VLM-based CBMs and their move into clinical imaging. We cover vision-language foundations (CLIP, ALIGN, LLaVA) and trace concept models from early supervised methods (CBM, CEM, TCAV) to versions that work without manual labels (LaBo, Label-Free CBM, PCBM, OpenCBM, VLG-CBM). We then map these foundations to specific medical fields such as radiology, pathology, cardiology, dermatology, and ophthalmology, highlighting the medical VLM-CBMs closest to actual deployment (CBVLM, AdaCBM, ConcepPath, CBM-RAG). We focus on information leakage, in which task information reaches the prediction through the concept layer without being carried by the named concepts. Two of the seven surveyed medical VLM-CBMs test whether their predictions depend on individual concepts, but none measures leakage, and no shared protocol exists. We identify this gap as a central challenge for interpretable medical AI.

title: Comparative Study of Deep Learning Architectures for Brain Tumour Classification
desc: Accurate and early classification of brain tumours from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is essential for treatment planning, yet many published deep learning studies are trained and tested on small, single-source datasets, reporting accuracies that may not hold outside these datasets. This study compares six deep learning architectures for four-class classification (healthy, meningioma, glioma and pituitary tumour): a baseline convolutional neural network (CNN), an attention-based CNN, ShuffleNet, and EfficientNet-B0, ResNet-50 and Xception augmented with the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM). The models were trained on a corpus assembled from four publicly available MRI datasets. Because these datasets carry no patient identifiers, a leakage-aware pipeline was developed that removes exact duplicates using MD5 hashing (550 images) and near-duplicates using perceptual hashing (8,024 images), and assigns visually similar images to the same fold during 5-fold group cross-validation. A leave-one-dataset-out (LODO) test on a fully held-out dataset was used to measure cross-dataset generalisation. Under a conventional random split, ShuffleNet achieved 97.1% accuracy with 1.2M parameters. Under leakage-aware group K-fold cross-validation, ShuffleNetV2 (98.41%) and EfficientNet-B0 (98.23%) were statistically indistinguishable (paired t-test, p = 0.19), and both significantly outperformed the custom CNNs. On the held-out dataset, accuracy dropped for every model: EfficientNet-B0 generalised best (78.4%), while ShuffleNetV2 fell to 66.2%. Glioma-meningioma confusion was the dominant error mode, and Grad-CAM maps showed that predictions were driven by tumour regions. These results indicate that in-distribution accuracy alone overstates real-world performance and that leakage-aware and cross-dataset evaluation should be reported alongside it.

title: Artificial intelligence and causation: from prediction to causal inference in biomedical research.
desc: [Journal of dentistry] To distinguish what dental artificial intelligence (AI) models demonstrate from what their findings are claimed to mean, and to offer a framework for matching each claim to the evidence required to support it. AI studies in dentistry report sensitivity, specificity, and area under the curve: measures of agreement between model outputs and a reference standard. Yet verbs such as predict, detect, identify, and explain are used interchangeably, and outputs are often read as identifying modifiable causes or as evidence of clinical benefit. Using the causal hierarchy of association, intervention, and counterfactual reasoning, this review separates description, prediction, causal effects of interventions, and individual counterfactuals. Directed acyclic graphs illustrate how confounding by indication can make an effective treatment appear harmful in a predictive model. The review summarizes the identification conditions that causal claims require (exchangeability, positivity, consistency) and where AI can legitimately contribute: measurement, nuisance-function estimation, heterogeneous treatment effects, and hypothesis-generating causal discovery. Model-explanation methods describe how a fitted model behaves, not how patients would respond to intervention. A published caries-detection model illustrates the evidence needed to move from diagnostic accuracy to claims about clinician decisions and patient outcomes. Most AI models developed for prediction operate at the association level. Model complexity and dataset size cannot substitute for a defined intervention, an appropriate design, and defensible identification assumptions. Dental AI accuracy studies show agreement with a reference standard, not that using the tool improves decisions or patient outcomes. Such claims require comparative evaluation of AI-assisted care.

title: EPPC-CARE: Staged Hierarchical Annotation of Communication Behaviors in Secure Patient-Provider Messages
desc: Objectives: Patient portal messages provide invaluable information about communication dynamics between patients and healthcare providers, but extracting it manually is labor-intensive. We developed and evaluated EPPC-CARE, an automated framework for identifying communication behaviors together with the supporting text for each classification. Materials and Methods: From 867 messages, we obtained 5,516 reference standard annotations. Each annotation is a triplet of communication-related text (span), a broader communication category (Code), and a specific subcategory (Sub-code). We evaluated EPPC-CARE's identified triplets across six open-weight large language models (LLMs) against supervised fine-tuning and communication-based models such as EPPC-OASIS. We also compared EPPC-CARE with human expert annotations on 100 messages. Results: EPPC-CARE improved performance over EPPC-OASIS across all six models. EPPC-CARE's Triplet F1 improved by 2.90 percentage points on average, with a best score of 64.4%. On the human expert evaluation subset, EPPC-CARE and the human expert showed comparable agreement with the reference standard, with differences favoring EPPC-CARE.
