Discussion: These findings suggest that identifying triplet components (span, code, subcode) sequentially can improve performance across model families while preserving the supporting text behind each identification. EPPC-CARE links the communication code and subcode with the source text (span), supporting human verification of automated annotations in clinical informatics. EPPC-CARE may therefore make larger-scale studies of patient-provider communication more feasible and provide a foundation for human-in-the-loop annotation workflows. Conclusion: EPPC-CARE offers a more reliable and reviewable approach for automated characterization of communication behaviors in secure patient-provider messaging.

title: Narrow-band imaging vs artificial intelligence for colonic surveillance in inflammatory bowel disease: a prospective, crossover study. Results from the CLEAR-IBD (colorectal lesion evaluation assisted by real-time AI in inflammatory bowel disease) trial.
desc: [Inflammatory bowel diseases] Artificial intelligence (AI)-based computer-aided detection (CADe) systems are increasingly used in colonoscopy but are trained mainly in non-inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) populations. The performance of AI-based CADe for detecting colitis-associated dysplasia compared with established imaging techniques remains unclear. This study compared colorectal dysplasia miss rates (DMR) between a non-IBD-trained CADe system (ENDO-AID CADe, Olympus) and narrow-band imaging (NBI) in patients with IBD undergoing surveillance colonoscopy. We conducted a unicentric, open-label, quasi-randomized crossover trial including IBD patients undergoing colorectal cancer surveillance. Each patient underwent colonoscopy with both CADe and NBI in alternating order. The primary outcome was the per-lesion DMR; a per-patient analysis was also performed. Sample size was pragmatically set at 60 patients based on previously published crossover studies comparing chromoendoscopy and NBI in this population. Sixty patients were included. In the per-lesion analysis, DMR was 42.9% (6/14) for NBI and 23.8% (5/21) for CADe (risk difference 19.0%; 95% CI, -11.2 to 46.9; P = .28). In the per-patient analysis, DMR was 16.7% (1/6) for NBI and 22.2% (2/9) for CADe (risk difference -5.6%; 95% CI, -40.8 to 37.2; P = 1.00). CADe detected more lesions overall than NBI (125 vs 75; P = .006), but a higher proportion were inflammatory (53.6% vs 13.3%; P < .001). NBI detected more hyperplastic lesions (66.7% vs 28%; P < .001). Dysplasia miss rates did not differ significantly between CADe and NBI, although wide CIs limit definitive conclusions and findings should be considered hypothesis generating. These results support further evaluation of AI as an adjunct to established endoscopic imaging, while highlighting the need for AI models specifically trained in IBD populations.

title: Train-Only-Constrained LM for Synthetic Clinical Trajectories: Leak-Safe Calibration and Auditable Dynamics
desc: Simulating clinical time series necessitates temporal realism, calibration that preserves model integrity, and privacy transparency. We present a train-only, constrained language-model pipeline that factorizes generation. A compact GPT-style language model learns cross-biomarker co-occurrence through quantile tokens, and temporal directions are enforced by 3x3 per-biomarker Markov transitions fit on TRAIN, allowing dynamics to be audited. We fit a monotone quantile map (QMap) on TRAIN only (SYN(TRAIN) -> SIM(TRAIN)); no TEST statistics are used. The fixed map is then applied to SYN(TEST) severities. The constrained LM demonstrated improved distributional fidelity and co-occurrence in a 5,000-patient simulated testbed (parameters within published clinical ranges) compared to an empirical sampler, maintained near-chance detectability after a small lambda-sweep, and exhibits temporal adherence by construction. A classifier-based membership-inference audit results in an AUC of approximately 0.5; we make no differential-privacy claim. We present multi-seed results with paired 95% confidence intervals and quantify the severity of QMap's alignment (Delta W1 with confidence interval). This is a Stage-1 method result obtained on a controlled simulator; Stage-2 validation on real EHR cohorts with clinical endpoints is planned.

title: Choosing the Right AI Model for Uveal Melanoma From Detection to Prognosis.
desc: [Clinical & experimental ophthalmology] Ocular oncology sits in an unusual position for medical artificial intelligence (AI), imaging heavy and multimodal by nature, but constrained by the rarity of the tumours it treats. Uveal melanoma, the most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults, accounts for approximately 7095 new cases worldwide each year. Choroidal naevi are present in approximately 5% of the white population aged 40 and over, of which roughly 1 in 8845 transforms into melanoma each year, leaving a large benign population within which a small number of melanomas must not be missed. This narrative review follows the uveal melanoma clinical pathway through detection, diagnosis and prognosis, asking at each stage which class of AI model the evidence supports. A structured PubMed search returned 176 unique records, from which 29 primary studies were included, 17 (59%) published in 2025 or 2026. At detection, heavy self-supervised foundation models generalise well across imaging hardware but lack calibration to a clinical decision, while lightweight purpose-built classifiers show the opposite trade-off, and only one tool has been tested in a real referral workflow, quadrupling the odds of correct referral and cutting false positives 10-fold. At diagnosis, purpose-built convolutional classifiers calibrated to a referral threshold remain most mature, reaching 0.88 AUC on two cohorts, while multimodal fusion claims rest on a single 0.01 AUC gain. At prognosis, biomarker prediction from routine pathology reaches 0.93 to 0.99 AUC, survival prediction lags, only 7 of 29 studies (24%) had external validation and none of the tools has regulatory clearance.

title: Cell-Type-Specific Expression Is Hard to Predict from Bulk, but It Is Still Useful
desc: Single-cell-informed deconvolution provides cell-type-resolved features for clinical bulk RNA cohorts. Most existing methods predict the proportions $π_k$ of the $K$ constituent cell types (CTs). Fewer predict cell-type-specific expression (CTSE) $μ_{kg}$ of gene $g$ in CT $k$, which can capture cell states that proportions miss, but recent benchmarks find it much harder. We explain this gap with closed-form accuracy bounds. For CTSE, we derive an $R^2$ ceiling for per-gene linear estimators. For proportions, the best linear estimator, which pools evidence across genes, has a closed-form $R^2$, and a computable lower bound on it predicts which CTs are learnable. We study targeted deconvolution of 106 biologically curated (CT, gene) pairs, found post hoc to have higher learnability scores. On overall survival in non-small cell lung cancer, estimation difficulty does not predict prognostic value across these targets. Yet a sparse survival model on deconvolved features, mostly CTSE, predicts survival as well as a sparse model on the bulk genes themselves, while attributing its signal to specific cell types. Some deconvolved CTSE features reveal prognostic signal not seen in the corresponding bulk gene.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Drug Development: Recent Advances and Emerging Applications.
desc: [Recent patents on nanotechnology] Drug research, formulation development, manufacturing, quality control, and pharmacovigilance are just a few areas of the pharmaceutical industry that have undergone a paradigm shift with the introduction of artificial intelligence (AI). The numerous ways that AI-driven technologies impact each stage of the pharmaceutical life cycle are examined in this comprehensive analysis. One subfield of machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) that stands out is deep learning (DL), which uses artificial neural networks (ANNs) to find intricate patterns and relationships in massive datasets by simulating the structure of the human brain. These methods have produced state-of-the-art results in fields such as speech detection, natural language understanding, image recognition, pharmacophore selection, and protein targeting. The manuscript discusses how data analytics, machine learning algorithms, and predictive modelling can be used to improve Pharmaceutical formulation development throughout its life cycle. This critical review provides important insights into the changing dynamics of drug development through AI-driven innovation by outlining the latest developments and patents.

title: EATS: Scaling Tool-Use Experience for Medical Reasoning Agents
desc: Medical reasoning agents combine large language model (LLM) reasoning with clinical workflows and specialized neural tools. However, general-purpose LLMs receive limited training exposure to domain-specific medical tools, and the uncertainty and distributional shifts of neural tool outputs make selecting tools from simple descriptions significantly more challenging than in deterministic settings such as calculators or dictionary lookups. In this paper, we propose EATS, an experience-augmented tool selection strategy that leverages accumulated tool-use trajectories to improve tool selection in medical reasoning agents. EATS constructs a memory of past interactions, including queries, tool choices, arguments, and self-evaluated feedback, and retrieves relevant experiences to guide tool selection for new queries. As memory construction does not require ground-truth supervision, EATS scales naturally with test-time experience. We evaluate EATS on tool-augmented medical reasoning tasks, including closed-ended visual question answering and free-form report generation. Experiments on four public datasets, ChestAgentBench, CheXbench, MIMIC-CXR, and SLAKE-VQA, across three multimodal LLMs, Qwen3-VL 2B, Qwen3-VL 32B, and GPT-5.5, show consistent gains in tool selection behavior and downstream medical reasoning performance. Code is available at https://github.com/Limingyuan001/EATS.

title: Data drift in clinical imaging AI: Medicolegal liability after deployment.
desc: [Clinical imaging] Data drift refers to changes in the distribution or characteristics of input data after deployment that may adversely affect the performance of artificial intelligence (AI) systems, even when the software continues to function exactly as designed. Patient demographics, disease prevalence, referral patterns, imaging protocols and technology continue to evolve after deployment, resulting in a divergence between the data distribution a model was trained on and the distribution it encounters in practice, without any discrete coding error or malfunction. These technical realities raise distinctive medicolegal questions when a patient is harmed by a degraded model. Establishing negligence centers on whether an ongoing institutional duty exists to monitor for performance deterioration, how breach can be proved absent consensus benchmarks for surveillance frequency and how causation can be demonstrated where AI output is only one element of clinical decision-making and its reasoning may be an opaque "black box" to its users. Comparative fault principles may allocate responsibility according to relative control and knowledge among institutions, vendors and radiologists. Products liability exposure and federal preemption laws also play a role. Risk reduction measures include lifecycle documentation, risk proportionate surveillance, auditability of algorithms and outputs, contractual allocation of monitoring responsibility, and sustained clinician oversight. Radiologists and institutions should anticipate a standard of care that evolves well before controlling case law develops.

title: PICE: Prototype-Informed Conditional Model Evolution Toward Self-Evolving Medical Image Recognition
desc: Medical image classifiers in clinical practice must continually evolve to accommodate emerging disease categories while maintaining reliable classification of existing conditions. This is challenging because privacy and data-sharing restrictions limit access to historical patient data, while assigning dedicated capacity to each new diagnostic task causes linear model growth. Effective evolution requires preserving prior disease knowledge without retaining historical images while expanding model capacity only when necessary. To this end, we propose PICE, a Prototype-Informed Conditional Model Evolution framework organized around what to preserve, when evolution is needed, and how that evolution is realized. PICE preserves prior disease knowledge in a prototype-statistical memory. For each incoming task, it assesses compatibility with historical references reconstructed from memory, reusing the closest adapter when compatibility is sufficient and instantiating a new one when evolution is required. PICE then realizes evolution by updating the memory and recalibrating the unified classifier with Gaussian pseudo features, thereby integrating new knowledge into the cumulative diagnostic space. During inference, memory-derived similarities guide task-agnostic adapter selection and fusion, enabling prediction over all learned disease categories. Experiments on Skin8, Kvasir-V2, and Path16 demonstrate the effectiveness of PICE across diverse clinical scenarios. On Skin8, PICE achieves a 7.60\% improvement in accuracy over the SOTA method on new tasks, while maintaining 71.10\% accuracy on previous tasks. It also reduces additional learnable parameters by 18.51\%. These results indicate that PICE improves classification while balancing knowledge retention, adaptation, and parameter growth, supporting continual model evolution as new diagnostic categories emerge without access to historical images.

title: The role of Artificial Intelligence in food allergy: A framework for navigating novel tools.
desc: [Journal of food allergy] Artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly penetrated health care and begun to influence clinical care, research, and health system operations. With food allergy, AI offers promise for clinical decision support, personalized care guidance, support of health literacy and a drive toward novel therapies. Despite growing enthusiasm, there are currently no U.S. Food and Drug Administration-cleared AI tools specifically indicated for food allergy, which underscores the need for a structured approach for evaluating, selecting, and implementing AI solutions within the domain. This narrative review focuses on a pragmatic framework for AI tool selection tailored to food allergy use cases. I review the current state of AI in health care and allergy/immunology, describe key dimensions of tool selection, including clinical question definition, data suitability, performance trade-offs, user interaction, governance, and sustainability, and illustrate how these considerations may be applied to food allergy-relevant challenges. By shifting attention from model novelty to problem-solution fit, implementation readiness, and long-term stewardship, this framework aims to support clinicians, researchers, and health systems to responsibly leverage AI for improved patient outcomes.

title: DDxBasis: Explaining Frozen Foundation Encoder-based Medical Classification by Exact Differential Diagnosis
desc: In differential diagnosis (DDx), a clinician explains a diagnosis by the few findings that separate it from the alternatives. Medical image classifiers cannot yet explain themselves this way. Existing explanations are either faithful but spread over hundreds of concepts, or compact but leave part of each decision unexplained. We present DDxBasis, which explains a classifier on a frozen foundation encoder as a differential diagnosis in three steps. First, a concept bottleneck reads all patch tokens at every encoder layer using gated, second-order slot attention. A concept basis then regroups the concepts into two-pole axes, each a differential between groups of diagnoses. Finally, we read a differential diagnosis from each axis through the typical presentation of its poles, the pertinent findings of the case, and counterfactual edits of borderline cases. Across five medical datasets, DDxBasis is the most accurate frozen-encoder model and close to the best published domain-specific results. Because every concept adds its own evidence, its reproducible concept basis splits each decision exactly, at no cost in accuracy. Without ordered stage or concept labels, the axes recover cell lineages and rare subtypes, agree with dermatologists' structure annotations, and expose planted and real shortcuts.

title: AI-driven transformation of GPCR research: from structural biology to precision medicine.
desc: [Frontiers in molecular biosciences] G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) regulate complex pathophysiological networks and represent a critical class of drug targets, but their structural determination and ligand screening are constrained by dependence on homology templates, static conformations, and a bias toward known ligands. Artificial intelligence is fundamentally transforming GPCR structural biology and pharmacology by overcoming these bottlenecks. The methodologies encompass high-precision static structure prediction, dynamic conformational ensemble modeling, ultra-large-scale virtual screening, de novo ligand design, allosteric mechanism decoding, biased signaling quantification, and systems pharmacology. Deep learning architectures enable end-to-end structure prediction exemplified by AlphaFold series, billion-compound virtual screening and unbiased de novo ligand design via diffusion models. Three-dimensional structure-aware Graph neural networks and molecular dynamics simulations are shifting research focus from single static conformations to transient conformations, cryptic allosteric sites, and ligand-induced biased signaling. Systems-level investigation through multi-omics-integrated GPCR digital twins advances personalized precision medicine. This review summarizes the innovative AI-driven paradigm, breaking traditional restrictions and greatly improving structural resolution of orphan receptors and GPCR complexes, thereby offering a comprehensive reference for dynamic GPCR pharmacological research. Core challenges include the black-box nature of deep learning, structural distribution biases, and the translational gap, which can be addressed by physics-informed models and high-throughput validation.

title: Do Not Let the Prior Heal the Anomaly: Selective Anchoring for Detection from Incomplete Measurements
desc: Generative priors can recover anatomical detail from incomplete medical measurements, but may erase the very lesions that imaging aims to detect, even when the measurements contain evidence of them. We introduce selective anchoring that protects reliably measured image components from prior-driven changes, while allowing expressive generative models to reconstruct unresolved structure. Acquisition uncertainty in the protected components is either added deterministically to the downstream test or carried by the ensemble through stochastic perturbations of the readings. We implement this principle as a wrapper for pretrained diffusion and flow samplers and as AnchoredFM, a fast constrained flow model. Under a linear-Gaussian measurement model, the protected coefficients are unbiased in expectation and achieve nominal interval coverage across repeated acquisitions, independently of the learned prior. Across sparse-view CT, accelerated brain MRI, and photoacoustic tomography, selective anchoring improves lesion contrast preservation and uncertainty reliability, and can reduce reconstruction error within lesions. For tumor detection in accelerated MRI, with a healthy reference estimated from the measurements alone, deterministic anchoring raises mean AUROC across eight samplers from 78.4% to 84.6% and lesion sensitivity at 0.25 false-positive marks per slice from 38.8% to 47.5%, with gains in all four predefined tumor-size groups. At thresholds frozen on healthy validation data, mean sensitivity rises from 20.2% to 44.1% (37.6% with stochastic anchoring). These findings show how expressive generative priors can reconstruct unresolved anatomy without healing away the abnormalities that the measurements support.

title: Utilizing AI Decision Support Tools in Burn Resuscitation: Comparing A Large Language Model to a Computerized Decision Support Tool.
source: PubMed · Journal of burn care & research : official publication of the American Burn Association
desc: [Journal of burn care & research : official publication of the American Burn Association] Crystalloid resuscitation is central to severe burn care. Traditional approaches rely on calculated formulae, monitoring, and endpoint guided titration. Computerized Clinical Decision Support (CDS) tools automate this process and improve goal-directed outcomes, but use remains limited due to accessibility. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer an unevaluated alternative. This study compared crystalloid estimates between a commonly used LLM and CDS system. A retrospective one-year two phase analysis was conducted for adult patients treated at an ABA-verified burn center who received individualized CDS-guided fluid resuscitation during the first 24 hours after injury. An LLM was queried using standardized prompts based on identical clinical inputs used by the CDS tool, including age, TBSA, weight, formulae, urine output, and confounders. Bland-Altman analysis assessed fluid volume predictions between the LLM and CDS system. This study included eighteen patients with a mean ± SD TBSA burn of 41.7% ± 20.2%, contributing 387 recommendations in Phase 1 and 380 in Phase 2. Mean LLM and CDS system rates through 24 hours post-burn were not statistically significant different (462 ± 318 mL/hr vs 450 ± 288 mL/hr; p=0.57). Correlation between the two systems was strong (r=0.93; 95% CI, 0.91-0.94, p<0.0001) with a mean difference of 12.3 mL/hr (95% limits of agreement, -222 to 246 mL/hr). Following prompt refinement, Phase 2 correlation remained strong (r=0.94; 95% CI, 0.93-0.95, p<0.0001) with a mean difference of -23.4 mL/hr and limits of agreement ranging from -178.3 to 131.5 mL/hr. LLMs can generate sequential fluid-rate recommendations during simulated burn resuscitation, but variability in fluid rates highlight the need for further refinement and clinical validation.

title: Automated Batch-Variable Selection for ComBat-Based Radiomic Harmonization
desc: ComBat harmonizes multicentre radiomic features, but batch variables are usually chosen manually, without a standardized criterion across image acquisition parameters. We propose ParsiComBat, which selects acquisition parameters for ComBat, balancing batch-effect removal against feature-structure preservation and abstaining when technical variation is negligible. ParsiComBat ranks candidate acquisition parameters by batch effect, filters redundancy, and scores sequential ComBat corrections. We evaluated it in three experiments: in simulations, testing whether it recovered a known batch variable and abstained without one; in CT (NSCLC-Radiomics) and MRI (MAMA-MIA) cohorts, comparing batch-effect removal against manufacturer (manual), every feasible parameter (greedy) and AutoCombat; and in clinical prediction, internally and externally. In simulations, ParsiComBat identified the true batch variable in 92.9% of positive trials and abstained in 99.2% of null controls. In CT, correcting for reconstruction kernel reduced mean k-nearest neighbour batch-effect test from 0.276 to 0.032, almost matching greedy correction of six variables. In MRI, correcting for slice thickness and manufacturer reduced it from 0.680 to 0.325, slightly more than manual selection but less than greedy correction of seven variables. Removing technical variation did not improve clinical discrimination: no strategy, including raw features, differed significantly from ParsiComBat in area under the curve. ParsiComBat provides a data-driven framework that removes technical batch effects using minimal acquisition parameters, preserving feature structure and clinical discrimination. It selects variables verifiable against the acquisition protocol and abstains when no correction is needed, supporting transparent, reproducible multicentre radiomics.

title: Updates in Diagnosis and Treatment of ATTR Cardiac Amyloidosis.
desc: [Current cardiology reports] This review summarizes the contemporary epidemiology, diagnostic approaches, screening strategies, and therapies for transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis (ATTR-CM), with emphasis on evolving diagnostic paradigms and emerging therapeutic targets. ATTR-CM is an under recognized yet treatable infiltrative cardiomyopathy with meaningful prevalence among patients with HFpEF, aortic stenosis, and select orthopedic conditions. Despite advances in noninvasive diagnosis and broader screening efforts, unacceptable delays in diagnosis remain rampant and continue to be an impediment to effective treatment. The expanding availability of disease-specific therapies, alongside a robust therapeutic pipeline, has heightened the clinical importance of earlier identification and intervention to improve outcomes. ATTR-CM is an increasingly recognized contributor to heart failure-related morbidity and mortality. Advances in screening, diagnosis, and disease-modifying therapies have begun to shift its disease course, underscoring the importance of timely detection and management.

title: Auditing Identity and Timing Signals in Operational Logs
desc: Models that predict events from operational logs, such as sepsis in ICU records or failures in hard drives, can score well by recognizing which patient or drive a record came from, or when it was recorded, instead of predicting the event. I introduce two simple audits that measure how much of this information a dataset carries before any event-prediction model is trained, and apply them to seven public datasets in six domains. One asks whether a classifier can tell that two records came from the same unit; the other asks which of two records from the same unit came later. Under the stated nulls, both have expected AUC 0.5. In ICU data, the identity audit flags a common preprocessing step: carrying the last measurement forward raises identity AUC from 0.916 to 0.993. On a 12-hour sepsis forecasting task, carrying forward makes a model look 0.163 AUC better than raw values when a patient's hours are split between training and test, but only 0.046 better when patients are held out. The exaggeration under patient overlap also appears in a second ICU dataset with mortality as the outcome. On the sepsis task, a chronological control with complete follow-up, in which training sees only a patient's earlier, resolved hours, shows no positive mean overlap gap. Timing is a strong predictor: with complete follow-up, hour of stay and measurement counts alone, with no clinical value, score 0.761 on held-out patients, and adding the raw clinical values changes that by +0.018. Outside the ICU, 95% of drives and 75% of loans have records on both sides of a calendar cut, and the overlap gap persists under a calendar split. The audits show which features and preprocessing choices to check; the evaluation protocol decides the consequences. I release the code, a library that runs the audits on any table with a unit column and a time column, and a guide to using the audits.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Exercise Prediction, Monitoring, and Personalization: A Systematic Review.
source: PubMed · Journal of functional morphology and kinesiology
desc: [Journal of functional morphology and kinesiology] Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to physiological prediction, physical activity monitoring, and personalized exercise prescription. However, evidence regarding its practical effectiveness remains heterogeneous. This systematic review examined applications of AI, machine learning (ML), and deep learning (DL) in exercise-related prediction, monitoring, and personalization among adults. Methods: Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, PubMed and Scopus were searched for studies published between 2015 and 2025, with Google Scholar used as a supplementary source. Eligibility followed PICO: adults aged 18 years or older (P); AI, ML, or DL applications for exercise prediction, monitoring, or personalization (I); conventional or non-personalized approaches, where applicable (C); and predictive accuracy and physiological, functional, or behavioral exercise outcomes (O). Findings were synthesized descriptively. Results: Ten studies were included: four examined physiological or energy-expenditure prediction, two investigated activity-related behavioral outcomes, two evaluated training-response classification or recommendation generation, and two assessed AI-personalized exercise interventions. Predictive models demonstrated promising performance in specific applications, although validation procedures and populations varied substantially. The intervention studies reported greater perceived exercise intensity and satisfaction in one trial and improvements in selected measures of balance, flexibility, and strength in another. Conclusions: AI-based approaches show potential for supporting exercise assessment, monitoring, and individualized decision-making. However, evidence regarding their superiority over conventional exercise prescription remains limited by the small number of intervention studies, methodological heterogeneity, and insufficient external validation. Further well-designed, long-term intervention studies are needed to establish their comparative effectiveness and practical benefits.

title: Feed-Forward Adaptive Gaussian Splatting for Interactive Medical Volume Rendering
desc: Path-traced rendering shows CT and MR volumes with realistic lighting, but it restarts after every change of view, clipping plane or transfer function (TF), the map from voxel intensity to colour and opacity, which limits the frame rate. Feed-forward Gaussian splatting models such as RenderFM predict the Gaussians directly from the volume instead of fitting them to each scan, and are fast. RenderFM, however, handles only CT, runs its network again after every TF edit, has no clipping operator, and places its Gaussians on a uniform 3-mm grid that blurs organ boundaries and cut faces. We present RenderFM-Next, a feed-forward model that addresses these limits. One network handles both CT and MR. Its Gaussians are predicted once per volume: a new TF needs no pass of this network, and a clipping plane cuts them exactly, using operators from prior work. The model predicts coarse 3-mm Gaussians for the whole volume and refines them to 1.5 mm only where refinement improves the image. A small score head ranks the coarse Gaussians by how much refining them would reduce the rendering error; at render time the user chooses how many are refined, and those next to a clipping plane are always refined, which sharpens cut faces. We build a benchmark of about 2,000 CT and MR scans with path-traced references under clinical presets, TF edits and clipping. Our RenderFM-Next improves over RenderFM retrained on this benchmark by 2.8 dB on CT and 2.4 dB on MR and renders a 1600x1600 view in 4-6 ms. Refinement adds 0.30 / 0.69 dB over the same model trained without it (0.51 / 1.17 dB on cut faces), and refining a learned 10% of the coarse Gaussians matches a random 50% with 2.4x fewer Gaussians. Project page: https://gaozhongpai.github.io/renderfmnext/

title: Single-cell Morphological Mechanisms-of-Action Profiling using Nanowell Imaging Plates.
source: PubMed · SLAS discovery : advancing life sciences R & D
desc: [SLAS discovery : advancing life sciences R & D] Mechanism-of-action (MoA) analysis is used in drug discovery to prioritize compounds that act through desired pathways while eliminating compounds associated with nonspecific or undesirable activity. Image cytometry provides a promising route for MoA inference by capturing high-dimensional cellular phenotypes at single-cell resolution, but conventional workflows remain limited by unreliable cell segmentation and dependence on human-engineered feature extraction. Here, we present a deep learning-based image cytometry workflow that confines single cells in nanowells to obtain uniformly framed, regularized single-cell images, enabling MoA inference directly from raw images without segmentation or human-engineered features. Using a nanowell-in-microwell platform, we treated cells with 21 chemotherapeutic compounds spanning 11 MoA classes across multiple doses and time points, generating more than 500,000 single-cell images for model training and validation. A ResNet-18 convolutional neural network trained on images annotated by known compound mechanism achieved 85% accuracy in MoA classification. When a second model was trained on compound identity rather than MoA, misclassification patterns frequently linked compounds with shared mechanisms, indicating that the model learned mechanism-level relationships directly from single-cell morphology, without those relationships being specified in advance. Together, these results establish regularized single-cell imaging in nanowells as a scalable and interpretable approach to image-based MoA classification that overcomes key limitations of segmentation-dependent feature analysis.

title: Mitigating Hallucinations in Medical Question Answering on ESC Cardiology Guidelines: Evaluation and Retrieval Optimization
desc: Background: Large language models produce hallucinations in medical question answering (QA). Verify-and-revise pipelines that check atomic claims against retrieved guideline evidence are a standard mitigation, but evaluations almost universally treat the verifier's output as ground truth, an assumption rarely tested. Objective: To measure, claim by claim against human judgement, how such a pipeline fails in a guideline-grounded clinical setting. Methods: We built a dataset of 160 questions (100 patient vignettes from 89 de-identified cases, 60 fact-based) over four recent ESC cardiology guidelines, all approved by a practising internist, and a retrieval corpus of 627 hand-verified guideline records at two chunk granularities. A five-stage pipeline was run under four retrieval configurations and three independent runs (1920 arm-runs); all 606 first-pass refuted claims were manually audited, an independent judge re-judged 906 decisions, and the expert blindly reviewed 100 accepted claims. Results: Only 44.7-50.6% of flagged claims were true hallucinations. Correction loops converged in 85.2-95.1% of cases, yet 35% of genuine final errors were introduced by correction. Single-run true-hallucination recall was 35.6-41.2%, the three-run union 71-80%; verifier agreement was moderate (kappa = 0.505). The blind probe estimated the accepted-claim miss rate at 3.2% (95% CI 0.7-6.7%). Final genuine-error rate: 1.7% of answers. Conclusion: Claim-level verification reduces hallucinated content by an order of magnitude, but verifier reliability, not generation, is the limiting factor and must be measured, not assumed.

title: Artificial intelligence in ophthalmology: a bibliometric analysis of current status, hot topics, and trends (2016-2025).
desc: [International journal of ophthalmology] To systematically analyze the current state of research, evolving trends, and future directions regarding the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in ophthalmology from 2016 to 2025, thereby providing a reference for researchers in this field. The Web of Science Core Collection database was searched, and journal publications related to AI in ophthalmology published between January 1, 2016, and December 31, 2025, were included. CiteSpace 6.3.1 was used to perform visual analyses of publication volume, distribution by country or region, research institutions and researchers, journal sources, keyword emergence, and high-impact publications. A total of 5798 research publications were included. The global annual publication volume showed a continuous upward trend, entering a period of stable growth after 2021. China ranked first globally with 1964 papers, followed by USA and India. University of London (204 papers), University College London (190 papers), and Sun Yat-sen University (190 papers) were the top three institutions by publication volume. Schmidt-Erfurth U (94 papers), Bogunovic H (86 papers), Yang WH (50 papers), and Wong TY (50 papers) were the leading researchers in terms of publication output. Research hotspots were highly concentrated on the automated screening and diagnosis of diabetic retinopathy (DR), with segmentation, retinal images, and feature extraction being the keywords with the highest growth rates. Analysis of high-impact papers further confirmed that DR screening is currently the most influential application scenario. Over the past decade, global research on AI in ophthalmology has developed rapidly, with China making particularly notable contributions in terms of publication volume. Research focus has shifted from traditional image processing methods to automated diagnosis using deep learning, with DR screening being the most mature application area.

title: MedSkill-E$^{2}$: Evaluating and Evolving Skills for Medical Agents
desc: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly use skills to access domain knowledge and complete real-world tasks. We observe that even when a skill specifies the rules and procedures needed for a task, agents may fail to apply them effectively during autonomous execution, a phenomenon we call skill Enable But Underuse (EBU). This issue is particularly consequential in medical tasks, where overlooking a single critical constraint can yield a plausible but incorrect result. To evaluate and address EBU, we introduce MedSkill-E$^{2}$, a framework for evaluating and evolving skills for medical agents. We construct EBU-Bench, a challenging benchmark covering 12 medically relevant task groups and associated skills, to evaluate agents' ability to use available skills autonomously. We quantify the EBU gap as the difference in skill-use accuracy between autonomous use and explicitly guided reading and application of the same skill. On EBU-Bench, all evaluated model-harness combinations exhibit EBU, with a mean gap of 43.94 percentage points (pp). For the same model, skill-use accuracy under autonomous use differs by up to 38.96 pp across harnesses. Motivated by these observations, we propose EBU-Evolve, which uses execution feedback from autonomous and explicitly guided skill use to distill effective guidance into reusable skill instructions. Relative to their pre-evolution versions, the revised skills improve skill-use accuracy during autonomous execution by 33.33 to 55.17 pp and continue to yield improvements when transferred across multiple models and harnesses. Our results show that autonomous skill-use accuracy varies across harnesses with the model and skill held fixed, and model rankings can change. EBU can persist even after a skill is opened. EBU-Evolve improves autonomous skill-use accuracy on unseen tasks within the same skill, with gains transferring across models and harnesses.

title: Can AI Accurately Estimate Nutrition From a Food Photo?
source: PubMed · Journal of medical Internet research
desc: [Journal of medical Internet research] Nutrition tracking can be a useful tool for achieving health and fitness goals, and AI photo features may help alleviate some of the burden of tracking food manually. In this News and Perspectives article, JMIR Correspondent Anna Zucker reports on the accuracy and potential trade-offs of these new AI features.

title: Weakly Conditioned Diffusion Model Augmentation for Prostate Segmentation
desc: Deep learning models for prostate MRI segmentation often struggle to generalize when trained on limited heterogeneous data, leading to boundary errors and over-segmentation. We present an augmentation framework using mask-conditioned synthetic and diverse T2-weighted MRI volumes to improve boundary precision and reduce over-segmentation. We employ a 2.5D weakly mask-conditioned denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) via channel concatenation. The diffusion model conditions on stacks of adjacent binary masks from training folds. The model generates T2 volumes consistent with the conditioning anatomy while diversifying tissue appearance. We evaluate the proposed approach on two cohorts of data: (i) the LUND probe cohort (n=432) for strategy selection and training nnU-Net from scratch with a 23% synthetic data mix, and (ii) the Medical Segmentation Decathlon (MSD) prostate cohort (n=32) evaluated with a 20% synthetic data mix. For the LUND cohort, we found that training an nnU-Net model from scratch with a 23% synthetic data mix reduced the mean false-positive voxels per case from 11,102 (baseline) to 10,757. On the MSD cohort, the augmented model with a 20% synthetic mix achieved a mean cross-validated Dice of 0.9094, improving over the baseline (0.8935) by 1.59 percentage points and reducing mean false-positive voxels by 23.1% (4,201 to 3,229). Experimental results on both these cohorts suggest that mask-conditioned DDPM augmentation can reduce over-segmentation errors and improve boundary adherence in data-constrained settings.

title: Evidence-Grounded Artificial Intelligence for Implant Treatment Planning: Development and Preliminary Evaluation of RAISE.
desc: [Journal of periodontal research] RAISE is an evidence-grounded, retrieval-augmented AI system integrating domain-specific evidence retrieval and structured clinical reasoning for implant treatment planning. In preliminary evaluations, RAISE-generated and RAISE-assisted resident treatment plans received higher expert ratings than their respective comparators, while RAISE assistance was associated with shorter planning time.

title: EGSE: Evidence-Grounded Skill Evolution for Medical Reasoning Agents
desc: Medical reasoning agents combine foundation models with specialized tools to interpret medical images, yet reusing their historical experience remains challenging. A correct final answer can conceal flawed reasoning or tool use, synthesized advice may lack source support, and superficially similar cases may require different diagnostic procedures. In this paper, we propose EGSE, an evidence-grounded skill evolution framework that distills historical dialogues from similar cases into reusable conditional workflows and progressively refines a multi-faceted skill library through supported and validated updates to improve medical agents. EGSE evaluates intermediate reasoning and tool use and contrasts repeated successful and failed rollouts to extract useful practices and evidence-supported avoidance guidance. These experiences are synthesized into workflows with applicability conditions and checks traceable to source dialogues. Library additions and merges require source-grounded review and execution validation. At inference time, EGSE routes queries to skill nodes organized by imaging modality, question task type, and disease category, then retrieves and selects applicable workflows based on their conditions, the current images, and the question to guide evidence acquisition and interpretation. Experiments across four chest X-ray benchmarks show that EGSE outperforms representative medical agents and skill evolution methods in reasoning accuracy while reducing tool calls. It also delivers consistent accuracy gains across seven foundation models and supports skill transfer across datasets.

title: Beyond Calcium: CT Phenotyping of Fibrocalcific Aortic Stenosis.
desc: [JACC. Cardiovascular imaging] Aortic stenosis is characterized by progressive fibrocalcific remodeling driven by inflammation, fibrosis, and calcification. Although echocardiography and noncontrast computed tomographic calcium scoring (aortic valve calcium score) remain the clinical standards for hemodynamic and structural assessment, computed tomographic angiography, already routinely performed for transcatheter aortic valve replacement planning, provides complementary tissue-level characterization of fibrotic and calcific valve remodeling. Artificial intelligence is increasingly being applied to facilitate the quantitative assessment of fibrocalcific burden and periaortic adipose tissue inflammation. This review examines emerging applications of computed tomographic angiography for fibrocalcific tissue characterization, inflammatory phenotyping, and artificial intelligence-enabled risk assessment in aortic stenosis and discusses their potential role in complementing conventional hemodynamic assessment.

title: Can Its Own Misses Teach an MLLM to Find Small Brain Metastases?
desc: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are becoming general readers of medical images, yet they remain weak at locating small abnormalities. Brain metastases expose this gap: at 384 px a 0.1 mL lesion covers less than a quarter of one visual token, and at one false positive per scan frontier MLLMs find fewer than 30% of lesions of 0.1-1 mL. Fine-tuning on one dataset helps but transfers poorly, and improving it further is slow trial and error steered by a single score. We introduce LANTERN (Lesion-finding AgeNt Through Error-driven Recursive learNing), a framework in which an MLLM improves recursively from its own misses. LANTERN recasts model development as an error-driven loop: a failure census attributes every missed lesion to one of four causes, an LLM mentor revises one of four levels (evidence acquisition, visual representation, learning policy, decision aggregation) per round, and a rule frozen before the first round decides what is kept, without test data and with every tool call audited. Over 15 unattended rounds, LANTERN raises a fine-tuned 4B MLLM from finding 75% to 94% of lesions at one false positive per scan on BraTS-MET, and 91% of those of 0.1-1 mL, compared with at most 51% and 29% for five frontier MLLMs read under the starting protocol; the gains hold on an external cohort (89%) and on unseen meningiomas (77%). These results show that an MLLM's own misses, attributed to their causes, can drive its reliable recursive self-improvement.

title: Deep Learning-Based Classification of Mandibular Growth-Rotation Phenotypes from Lateral Cephalometric Radiographs: A Comparative Evaluation of Convolutional Neural Networks.
desc: [Dentistry journal] Background/Objectives: The cross-sectional classification of mandibular growth-rotation morphology is relevant to orthodontic diagnosis and treatment planning, but conventional structural assessment is observer-dependent. This study developed and internally evaluated deep learning models for classifying existing clockwise and counterclockwise mandibular growth-rotation phenotypes on lateral cephalometric radiographs; it did not forecast future longitudinal growth. Methods: Eight hundred untreated radiographs from individuals aged 9-20 years were labelled by consensus using Björk and Skieller morphological indicators (clockwise, n = 376; counterclockwise, n = 424). A stratified 80:20 training-validation split was used. ResNet50, InceptionV3, and VGG16 were fine-tuned after Gaussian noise reduction, min-max normalisation, and limited geometric augmentation. Results: VGG16 showed the most favourable validation accuracy-loss profile. The archived aggregate confusion matrix (n = 800) yielded an apparent accuracy of 81.13% (95% CI, 78.38-83.75) and balanced accuracy of 81.32% (95% CI, 78.62-83.96); recall was 84.57% for clockwise and 78.07% for counterclockwise phenotypes. Because the matrix included the complete labelled cohort, these values are descriptive apparent performance and not an independent test estimate. Conclusions: VGG16 can classify cross-sectional mandibular growth-rotation phenotypes with promising apparent performance. External, longitudinal, and observer-benchmark validation is required before clinical use.

title: Look at What Matters: Learning Lesion Prototypes from Severity Labels for Domain-Generalized Diabetic Retinopathy Grading
desc: Deep learning models for diabetic retinopathy (DR) grading often generalize poorly to unseen imaging domains, in part because predictions may exploit correlations specific to source datasets rather than retinal pathology. We address this challenge by constructing grading decisions from lesion evidence learned using only image severity labels. Clinical implications of DR grades provide multiple instance constraints that guide competitive learning of lesion and background prototypes at multiple scales. An additive ordinal scoring model then predicts severity exclusively from individual lesion prototype responses, explicitly connecting learned evidence with grading decisions without a global feature classification pathway. To improve the reliability of this evidence, we introduce teacher guided preservation under image degradations and spatial regularization against persistent coordinate preferences. Across six public DR datasets under a leave one domain out protocol, our method attains a mean quadratic weighted kappa of 0.761, outperforming the strongest competing method by 0.036. Localization and prototype removal analyses show that the learned responses align with retinal lesions and contribute to grading decisions. Experiments across five other prototype architectures and under image degradations further demonstrate the generality and robustness of the approach.

title: GRLV: Gradient reversal layer with variance loss for major depressive disorder detection.
desc: [Journal of neural engineering] Deep learning models have been widely applied to predict major depressive disorder (MDD) using magnetoencephalography (MEG) signals. However, these models often suffer from limited performance and generalization. This is primarily due to the strong individual heterogeneity inherent in MEG temporal signals, which makes it difficult for models trained on small samples to distinguish disease-related features and individual-specific features. To address this issue, we propose GRLV, a plug-and-play framework based on gradient reversal layer with variance loss, that can be readily embedded into existing deep learning classification models. This framework introduces a variance loss function to the gradient reversal layer (GRL) framework to compensate for its convergence limitations. We evaluated GRLV on 10 backbone models, achieving an average classification accuracy of 68.2%, and surpassing baseline models by 3.5%. Visualization results prove that the GRLV framework effectively attends to bilateral occipital activities within the first 100 ms post stimulus on-set, which is associated with the early processing of negative emotional faces in MDD patients, and is a better disease marker due to less contamination from individual heterogeneity. These findings fully demonstrate the broad application potential of GRLV in existing MEG/EEG decoding models and the discovery of mental diseases. These findings fully demonstrate the broad applicability of GRLV on existing MEG/EEG decoding models and its potential for advancing the discovery of biomarkers of mental disorders.

title: DoseSteer: Steering diffusion-based dose prediction models towards clinical targets via Dual-Response Guidance
desc: AI dose-prediction models generate patient-specific 3D dose distributions from patient anatomy. Yet these predictions can still miss structure-level clinical dose targets. Once deployed, most existing predictors offer no direct mechanism to correct such deviations, deferring target enforcement to downstream plan optimization. We introduce DoseSteer, an inference-time framework that steers frozen diffusion-based dose prediction models towards specified clinical targets without retraining. To meet clinical targets while preserving overall dose prediction quality, we propose Dual-Response Guidance (DRG), a structure-centric algorithm that probes the model's responses to perturbations in each structure's noisy dose and context and jointly solves for per-structure steering strengths. Across five dataset-model configurations spanning three diffusion architectures and three datasets, DRG outperforms 12 training-free baselines under identical reference-derived target proxies, removing at least 97% of the target error, reducing the official dose error by 7.8% on average, and improving dose fidelity outside the steered structures. DoseSteer reconciles learned anatomical dose priors with explicit structure-level targets at test time, establishing a principled, training-free mechanism to refine AI dose predictions prior to plan optimization. Code is available at https://github.com/csp2002/DoseSteer.

title: Integrating artificial intelligence across the drug safety lifecycle: mapping the gaps.
desc: [Drug discovery today] Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used during the drug safety lifecycle, but integration across the lifecycle remains challenging. It is not yet known whether AI can be used cohesively to enhance safety predictions by connecting discrete stages of drug development. Here, we review the performance of AI within four separate domains; absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion (ADME), toxicity, drug-drug interactions (DDIs), and pharmacovigilance (PV). We then evaluate putative cross-domain (translational) bridges. While reported within-domain performance is often high, validation on external data sets remains uncommon. Importantly, cross-domain information transfers are less frequently tested, meaning that evidence for translational bridges improving prediction remains rare. Therefore, more reliable end-to-end safety assessment will require harmonised endpoints, prespecified validation strategies, and greater interdisciplinary collaboration.

title: What, Who, and When: Structured Harm Assessment for Mental Health Safety via Short Reasoning
desc: The growing use of large language models (LLMs) for mental health support raises important safety concerns. Existing guard models primarily identify categories of harmful content, often overlooking the context needed to determine an appropriate response. We introduce a clinically grounded taxonomy that characterizes harm along three dimensions: what the harm is, who is involved, and when it occurs. It further separates harm characterization from intervention decisions, thus enabling safety policies to be specified outside the model weights through explicit, clinician-curated instructions that can be updated and audited. We validate the taxonomy with expert clinicians and validate a panel of LLM judges to scale annotation. Relabeling public benchmarks in this taxonomy shows that they rarely contain harm directed at the user, which accounts for nearly half of the harm in real conversations. We then train MindGuard2, a 35B-A3B reasoning-based guard model using supervised fine-tuning on short reasoning traces followed by reinforcement learning with a reasoning-length penalty, to minimize inference overhead while preserving the benefits of reasoning. On two public benchmarks and real-world conversations, MindGuard2 achieves balanced accuracy comparable to the substantially larger GLM-5.3 at approximately 10x lower median latency, advancing the accuracy-latency Pareto frontier. Furthermore, it achieves low false-positive rates at high recall, helping balance the need to detect unsafe situations against the risk of unnecessary interventions that may disrupt support and undermine user trust. We release a safety guardrail model with SOTA performance trained on synthetic data, together with synthetic conversations and annotations of public benchmarks in our taxonomy.

title: BERTE: hierarchical classification of transposable elements via multi-scale BERT-based representations.
desc: [Briefings in bioinformatics] Transposable elements (TEs) are major components of eukaryotic genomes and play important roles in genome evolution and regulation, yet their accurate classification remains difficult because TE categories are hierarchically organized and many sequences are highly redundant or homologous. This redundancy can inflate reported performance if closely related elements are shared across data partitions, making reliable generalization assessment a central challenge in TE classification. To address these challenges, we propose BERTE, a hierarchical TE classification framework designed for robust prediction under similarity-controlled evaluation. BERTE combines multi-scale contextual sequence representations with protein-domain evidence and performs taxonomy-consistent prediction through a hierarchical classifier. Using a large curated benchmark constructed from 13 public TE databases with similarity-aware clustered splitting, BERTE achieves strong performance among the evaluated TE-specific, general-purpose sequence-modeling, machine-learning, and homology-based methods across hierarchical and level-specific metrics and demonstrates strong generalization on multiple independent test datasets. Overall, BERTE establishes a robust and generalizable framework for hierarchical TE classification, providing a principled solution for accurate and reliable TE classification in large-scale genomic studies.

title: A gene informed benchmark for BioScoring of pathology foundation models
desc: Pathology foundation models are usually compared by their performance on downstream tasks such as classification and retrieval. While such benchmarks measure how useful a model is, they provide no insight into the biology it represents. We introduce BioScore, a benchmark that quantifies how well an image encoder captures cell identities, with spatial transcriptomics of the same tissue as the reference. A sparse autoencoder splits the encoder's patch embeddings into sparse features, which we cluster into a fixed number of groups. BioScore then measures, for each of 52 cell identities defined by marker genes, how specifically one group follows the identity's expression over the tissue. Because the autoencoder training is fully unsupervised, a match shows that the model represents the cell identity from the image alone. We score 8 pathology foundation models and 3 natural-image models. Every pathology model scores above every natural-image model (0.299--0.371 \vs 0.214--0.232), and paired tests separate three tiers among the pathology models. Unlike a supervised probe, BioScore needs no labels, builds its reference from the data and scores even from few sections, yet it ranks the encoders as a probe does. Its per-identity breakdown indicates which cell identities each encoder captures or misses.

title: Deep Learning-Assisted Highly Sensitive Hydrogel Sensors for Underwater Breaststroke Motion Recognition.
desc: [ACS applied materials & interfaces] Ion-conductive hydrogels hold immense promise for flexible electronics, but their inherent swelling in liquid environments severely limits amphibious applications. Herein, a highly conductive, anti-swelling hydrogel designated as PASLC was developed via the one-pot photo-initiated copolymerization of acrylic acid (AA), lauryl methacrylate (LMA), sulfobetaine methacrylate (SBMA), and cetyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB). When the molar ratio of hydrophilic to hydrophobic monomers was optimized to 150:3, the resulting PASLC-3 hydrogel achieved optimal swelling equilibrium, with a swelling ratio of only 4% after 7 days of immersion in water. Concurrently, this microenvironment effectively mitigates ion leakage and facilitates dynamic strain-induced conductive pathways, yielding an unprecedented seawater gauge factor (GF) of up to 12.974, which surpasses the value obtained in air. Furthermore, the hydrogel exhibits excellent stretchability (751.80% fracture strain), durable multi-substrate adhesion underwater, and superior biocompatibility (97% L929 cell viability at 24 h). Benefiting from this holistic design, PASLC-3 reliably enables real-time motion monitoring and Morse code transmission even after 7 days of seawater soaking. Integrated with deep learning neural networks, this sensor precisely decodes breaststroke kinematics, providing an attractive paradigm for robust, anti-swelling amphibious human-machine interfaces.

title: Sage-Med: Scaling Medical Multimodal Intelligence
desc: Establishing effective scaling laws for medical multimodal large language models (MLLMs) remains a persistent and fundamental challenge. Our systematic evaluation shows that existing medical MLLMs tend to underperform frontier general-purpose MLLMs across a range of medical tasks, while scaling model size primarily improves text capabilities rather than multimodal perception, and enabling reasoning modes fails to close this visual gap. To investigate how medical multimodal intelligence scales in practice, we introduce Sage-Med-Preview, a 35B-parameter medical multimodal model with 3B activated parameters, built by combining stage-specific curation over 322.7 million candidate records with a progressive training curriculum spanning medical pretraining, staged supervised fine-tuning, and adaptive reinforcement learning. Across this curriculum, progressive supervised refinement and adaptive reinforcement learning yield consistent stage-wise gains, substantially advancing both specialized visual understanding and medical language capabilities. Evaluated against 77 competing models across 238 clinical tasks spanning 61 public and 13 private multi-center benchmarks in more than 40 modalities, Sage-Med-Preview achieves an average score of 58.26% on the 31 public multimodal benchmarks. It outperforms the state-of-the-art open-source medical model Hulu-Med-235B-A22B at 50.99% and the general scientific model Intern-S2-Preview at 52.24%, and approaches the advanced proprietary model GPT-6.2-Sol across multiple tasks such as comprehensive multimodal understanding, report generation, and visual grounding. Although substantial challenges remain in complex medical reasoning and multi-step clinical workflows, this report provides empirical evidence, actionable data and training recipes, and a rigorous benchmark toward scalable clinical multimodal intelligence.

title: IsoVEM: Accurate and robust isotropic reconstruction with defects section inpainting for volume electron microscopy.
desc: [Structure (London, England : 1993)] Volume electron microscopy (vEM) provides 3D nanoscale imaging of biological ultrastructure but faces a key limitation: anisotropic resolution, where the axial detail is markedly inferior to the lateral detail. Existing deep learning solutions lack stability, compromise structural continuity, and fail to address practical slice defects. We present IsoVEM, a robust deep learning method for high-fidelity isotropic vEM reconstruction. Utilizing a video Transformer architecture, IsoVEM captures long-range cross-slice dependencies to maintain structural continuity and delivers accurate reconstructions under significant anisotropy. This helps overcome a major bottleneck in large-scale, high-throughput ultrastructural analysis. As a self-supervised model, IsoVEM requires no pre-existing isotropic training data and generalizes well, outperforming state-of-the-art techniques across four vEM modalities. In a landmark application, IsoVEM successfully resolves the complete 3D ultrastructure of mouse sperm in seminiferous tubules, yielding unprecedented insights into organelle assembly and maturation.

title: Rank Before You Encode: Reading a Few Percent of a Whole-Slide Image
desc: Classifying a whole-slide image requires encoding thousands of high-resolution tiles with a pathology foundation model, which accounts for most of the inference cost. Existing efficient methods reduce this cost by selecting fewer tiles, but typically train a new model around their selection strategy. A largely unexplored alternative is to keep an existing full-bag model frozen and run it on selected tiles at the same encoder cost. We introduce this comparison, alongside random tile sampling at matched cost. To select tiles, we fit a lightweight selector with 3.3K parameters to the attention of a frozen model, without additional slide labels. The selector ranks regions from a slide thumbnail, encodes the top K regions at 5x magnification, and selects b for processing at 20x. We evaluate seven frozen MIL aggregators on six tasks and compare them with nine efficient methods trained on the same features and splits. At a budget of (K,b)=(1000,10), encoding costs about 6.6% of the full bag and is 10-14x faster, excluding tiling. The AUROC drop is no more than 0.005 in 33 of 36 aggregator-task pairs. At (500,10), the cost falls to about 4% and inference is 13-22x faster, but AUROC drops by up to 0.035 on CAMELYON17, where small metastases are easily missed. Selection improves over random sampling by about 0.10 AUROC on tasks with focal lesions, while random sampling performs well on diffuse tasks. In our comparisons, the frozen model at (500,10) is ahead of nine efficient methods in 55 of 60 paired comparisons. Giving an existing WSI model fewer tiles is thus a baseline that a new efficient model should be compared with at matched encoder cost.

title: Interpretable identification of constitutive parameter field for three-dimensional heterogeneous and graded hyperelastic materials from full-field displacements
desc: The inverse problem of identifying spatially varying material properties of heterogeneous solids using experimentally available displacement fields and boundary reaction forces alone remains challenging. Being able to characterize heterogeneous and graded solids would be advantageous in the design and manufacturing of functionally graded materials and composites. Additionally, an efficient technique for identifying heterogeneous material properties from in vivo measurements would be useful in biomedical contexts to characterize heterogeneous biological tissues. Although several techniques developed over the past two decades have addressed inverse identification for homogeneous materials, including linear elastic, hyperelastic, viscoelastic, and elastoplastic solids, comparatively fewer studies have considered heterogeneous and graded materials. Furthermore, several recent approaches to characterizing heterogeneous and graded materials employ parameter-heavy, deep learning-based frameworks trained to enforce force equilibrium at specified collocation points within the material. In this work, we propose an interpretable and time-efficient framework that predicts the three-dimensional relative spatial variation of a constitutive parameter field for multiple parameters of a heterogeneous hyperelastic material, using only displacement-field data. In this work, we validate our framework on 3D synthetic and 2D experimental benchmarks involving heterogeneous, graded, and anisotropic hyperelastic materials. By leveraging the linear nature of the inverse problem for hyperelastic materials and directly optimizing for the constitutive parameters at the finite-element level, we achieve acceptable prediction accuracy with significantly lower computational time compared to recently reported deep-learning-based frameworks.

title: Multi-view fnirs identifies neurophysiological subtypes in post-stroke aphasia
desc: Post-stroke aphasia is clinically heterogeneous, and conventional classifications may not capture differences in brain functional organisation. We tested whether resting-state and task-based functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) could identify neurophysiological subgroups alongside clinical assessment.Seventy-nine patients underwent unsupervised clustering using three fNIRS feature views: resting-state activity and connectivity, language-task activation, and rest-to-task connectivity reconfiguration. Similarity network fusion and spectral clustering integrated the views. Clinical and behavioural measures were excluded from clustering.Three clusters (n = 32, 17 and 30) were identified. This solution had the largest eigengap and was the only candidate significant after permutation testing and Holm correction (adjusted P = 0.001). It was stable under subsampling (mean adjusted Rand index, 0.773), but agreement fell to 0.217 when the resting-state view was removed. Clusters differed in most regional intrinsic-activity measures and all resting-state connectivity summaries, with few differences in task activation or connectivity reconfiguration. Their profiles showed higher right anterior prefrontal activity, distributed fronto-sensorimotor and parietal alterations, and reduced interhemispheric connectivity, respectively.Cluster membership was not significantly associated with conventional aphasia subtype (Cramér's V = 0.287), and baseline clinical language scores and task performance did not differ between clusters.These findings identify three neurophysiological subgroups distinguished mainly by intrinsic activity and resting-state functional connectivity, not clearly aligned with conventional aphasia classifications or baseline clinical measures. Multi-view fNIRS analysis may complement clinical characterisation, requiring independent and longitudinal validation.

title: Where Does Free-Text 3D Grounding Fail? An Error Analysis of Report-Sentence Segmentation in Chest CT
desc: Free-text 3D grounding, segmenting in a CT volume the region described by one sentence of the radiology report, could link reports to images at scale, but it is unclear where current models fail. We analyse the publicly released VoxTell model on all 381 findings of the 200-scan ReXGroundingCT validation set, where it grounds 53.5% of findings. Its failures are rarely about which lesion or side is meant. No miss lies on the side opposite to the one named, and findings are almost never confused with one another. Instead, predictions are too large, land on a neighbouring lesion on the correct side, or are missing for small findings, and diffuse findings are rarely grounded. Removing location words halves performance, to the level of label-only prompting, and anatomical rules derived from the sentence never improve the full-sentence output. The same pattern holds on the hidden 300-scan test set. Further progress therefore depends on extent estimation and small-lesion sensitivity rather than on anatomical post-processing.

title: Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Immediate and Prospective Credit Assignment for Medical Visual Reasoning
desc: Medical visual question answering (VQA) requires acquiring useful evidence and deciding where to look next. Yet final-answer rewards do not reveal which observations support answering or guide subsequent inspection. We introduce MedPACT, an agentic reinforcement learning framework that learns selective observation policies through immediate answer support and prospective guidance. Our content-controlled estimator compares next actions induced by real and matched alternative observations under a shared real-observation history, isolating how observed content improves subsequent decisions. We combine both forms of credit within GRPO, assigning observation credit to the corresponding tool-call tokens alongside trajectory-level outcome supervision. MedPACT uses a single vision-language model and image-question-answer supervision, with credit estimation confined to training. Experiments with 4B and 8B backbones on six medical VQA benchmarks demonstrate improved accuracy, strong out-of-distribution generalization, and substantially lower inference costs. Case studies further illustrate how MedPACT avoids repeated observations and uses acquired evidence to guide subsequent inspection, demonstrating real-world practice potential.

title: Structure-Aware Multimodal Retrieval Under Data Scarcity, Privacy Constraints and Out-of-Domain Content
desc: Purpose: Figure retrieval from reference atlases in expert domains like forensic pathology, dentistry and geology must work without labels or training pairs, on content that often cannot leave local hardware, and on images outside the training data of image-text encoders. This work proposes a structure-aware pipeline that satisfies all three, retrieving figures through the page structure recovered by layout geometry and a local open-weight 8B VLM. Methods: A geometry-based pairing method is introduced, in which the model receives a schematic of the detected boxes and selects each picture's caption without access to pixels or text. Caption retrieval is evaluated on three private corpora (29 books, 10,421 figures, 218 queries) with blind human grading, against a lexical baseline, generated descriptions and five image-text encoders. Results: Geometric pairing was correct for 96%, 92% and 77% of pictures in the three domains, against 76%, 45% and 53% for the better of two document parsers. A hosted model given the schematic was equally accurate, while coordinates as text lost 22 points. Caption retrieval obtained an nDCG@5 of 0.85, 0.87 and 0.76, against 0.54, 0.51 and 0.27 for the best cross-modal encoder and 0.41, 0.28 and 0.30 for generated descriptions. Pairing errors carried over to retrieval. Conclusion: The proposed pipeline achieves accurate figure retrieval with small local models and no in-domain training, where general and biomedical image-text encoders fall far behind. Its geometry-only pairing is the most accurate of five methods and exposes no content, even to a hosted model. Code and prompts are released.

title: BreathSplat: Grounding One Smooth Motion in the Breathing Phase for 4D Cone-Beam CT
desc: Four-dimensional cone-beam computed tomography (4D-CBCT) images the anatomy of a breathing patient, but sees each breathing phase from only a few angles. Breathing, however, is a smooth motion that repeats; it has a phase. Existing methods exploit this either by reconstructing the anatomy as a function of the breathing phase, often through bins, or by estimating smooth dynamic motions in time. Yet none of these grounds one smooth motion in the phase. We thus propose to share projections across breathing phases with splines. Specifically, we represent the 4D volume with dynamic Gaussians whose motion uses B-splines in space and time. We ground the motion state in the respiratory phase, which we read from well-studied conventional surrogates. Projections at the same phase in different breathing cycles then constrain the same anatomy and motion. On simulated lung scans, our method, BreathSplat, outperforms recent dynamic methods in reconstruction and motion accuracy, including those given the ground-truth phase. We further show qualitatively, on two real patient scans, that our method provides clearer reconstructions than the state of the art.

title: Typical Angina, Reversed: A Long-Standing Documentation Error in the UCI Heart Disease Data
desc: The UCI Heart Disease data are a widely used machine-learning benchmark. We show that their chest-pain variable is stored in reverse of its documentation. At all four sites, the code documented as "asymptomatic" (4) marks patients with typical angina, and the code documented as "typical angina" (1) marks patients with almost none of the classical angina features (at Cleveland, no chest pain). Two complementary checks establish this: (i) the chest-pain table and regression coefficients of the original 1986 Cleveland study are reproduced only under the corrected reading; (ii) in the Budapest, Switzerland and Long Beach files, 93-96% of patients coded 4 have all three classical angina features. A 1990 word-labeled Cleveland file already uses the documented labels, and Statlog (Heart), a Cleveland subset, stores the same codes. OpenML, PMLB and two highly voted Kaggle copies that name the categories use the same documented labels (about 400,000 downloads combined). We audited a seeded random sample of 150 records from a pre-specified Scholar query for SHAP studies of these data mentioning asymptomatic chest pain (124 readable). Of 32 papers that state a direction for a named category, 25 (78%; 95% CI 61-89%) state one inconsistent with the corrected category identities; 22 (69%; 51-82%; post hoc) are attributable to the documentation error, and nine of these explain it clinically. None of the 124 readable papers identifies the reversal. Conventional models are essentially unaffected, one reason the error went unnoticed. Interpretations that attach the documented names to model effects are reversed, and zero-shot language-model classifiers that read the labels are misled: with the documented labels, three open-weight models lose 0.12-0.33 in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) given age, sex and chest-pain type. We give the corrected mapping, evidence and code.

title: Beyond Pose Control: Anatomically Consistent Ultrasound Video Generation
desc: Camera-controlled video generation anticipates how a scene appears from new viewpoints by relying on a prior learned implicitly from large-scale data. Ultrasound poses the same problem, with the probe pose as the viewpoint, but under opposite conditions: anatomy offers an explicit prior that every sonographer relies on, whereas tracked scans are too scarce to learn it implicitly. As a result, pose control alone is not enough, and pose-conditioned ultrasound generators produce implausible anatomy in unscanned regions and inconsistent anatomy on revisits. We go beyond pose control and give the generator the two kinds of knowledge that make up a sonographer's mental model. An anatomical prior, built from a population of subjects, guides generation where nothing has been scanned, and is refined online by every generated chunk towards the scanned subject. A 3D latent memory, designed around the cross-sectional physics of ultrasound, compounds the generated slices into a volume of the patient and reslices it at new poses, keeping revisited anatomy consistent. The fine-grained memory enters the generator at the input, while the coarse anatomy prior guides the layout across transformer blocks. Experiments on thyroid, kidney, and lumbar spine show improved visual fidelity, pose following, and anatomical consistency over pose-conditioned and memory-augmented baselines.

title: Structured Noise Diffusion for Echocardiography Haze Removal
desc: Echocardiographic images are frequently degraded by spatially structured haze artifacts that obscure anatomical boundaries and hinder clinical analysis. Conventional diffusion models typically employ pixel-independent Gaussian noise, limiting their ability to represent localized ultrasound haze. In this study, we propose a structure-informed diffusion framework that explicitly models ultrasound haze as an accumulation of localized Gaussian components constrained by the ultrasound fan geometry. The forward process generates spatially correlated corruption by sampling component locations and scales, providing a formulation that better reflects the spatial characteristics of real echo artifacts. During reverse restoration, a dual-head network predicts an anchor probability map and Gaussian scale parameters to progressively remove structured artifacts while reducing the center bias associated with direct coordinate regression. We evaluated the framework on the public DehazingEcho2025 benchmark and two private clinical datasets, without retraining or fine-tuning on either private cohort.
